# <mark>Lower Lip Squamous Cell Carcinoma</mark>

<mark>Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lower lip typically arises in the setting of chronic sun exposure and often begins as a roughened papule within actinic cheilitis or as scaly leukoplakia, progressing slowly to a tumor nodule.</mark> <mark>Clinical features suggestive of evolving SCC include persistent lip chapping with localized scale or crust, a red and white blotchy atrophic vermilion zone, an indistinct or "wandering" vermilion border, and small fissures or ulcerations within an area of indurated actinic cheilitis.</mark>

<mark>Pain or altered sensation should prompt evaluation for possible perineural invasion, which is more common in advanced lesions of the head and neck, including the lip.</mark>

<mark>It may also present as a peritonsillar abscess when associated with metastatic spread or regional involvement.</mark>

# <mark>Genital Squamous Cell Carcinoma</mark>

SCC of the vulva most commonly arises on the anterior labia majora and may present as a small warty nodule or an erosive erythematosus plaque. These lesions may be asymptomatic but are more often associated with pruritus or bleeding. Precursor conditions include lichen sclerosus. 

Cervical SCC is strongly associated with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly HPV type 16.

SCC of the scrotum typically begins as a small pruritic verrucous lesion that becomes friable as it enlarges.

Penile SCC usually occurs in uncircumcised males and is rare in Western countries but may account for up to 10% of cancers in regions with poor genital hygiene. A key precursor is erythroplasia of Queyrat, characterized by a velvety red plaque. Risk factors include lack of circumcision, history of genital condyloma, phimosis, and lichen sclerosus et atrophicus.

Although genital SCC was once reported following long-term psoralen and UVA (PUVA) therapy, this risk has been minimized by shielding the genital area during treatment, making such cases rare today.

Perianal SCC can also occur and may be associated with HPV infection or chronic inflammatory conditions.

# Scar Squamous Cell Carcinoma

SCCs arising in scars typically develop decades after the initial injury, often presenting with skin breakdown, persistent erosion, or ulceration. These are most commonly found on the lower extremities at sites of chronic venous insufficiency or pyogenic granuloma ulcers.

Nodularity may develop gradually, but detection is often delayed due to concealment by surrounding indurated scar tissue. In cases arising within chronic sinuses, nodularity may be absent. New or increasing pain, drainage, or bleeding in a chronic scar should raise suspicion for malignant transformation and warrants biopsy.

# Keratoacanthoma

(For full discussion, see Chapter 113.)

# II.1. Risk Factors for Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

## <mark>II.1.1. Environmental and Exogenous Factors</mark>

<mark>The occurrence of SCC is associated with total cumulative lifetime UV dose.</mark> <mark>The most commonly affected sites include the face, back of the hands, and forearms.</mark> <mark>In a Spanish study, more than 92% of SCC cases occurred in these areas.</mark> <mark>UVB (290–320 nm) and UVA (320–400 nm) both play a role in carcinogenesis.</mark> <mark>For most SCCs, UV-induced mutations are observed in the *P53* gene.</mark>

<mark>Artificial sources of UV radiation have also been implicated.</mark> <mark>PUVA therapy, particularly when exceeding 200 sessions, is associated with an increased risk of SCC.</mark> <mark>Tanning salon UV sources are not harmless and must be considered among other risk factors.</mark> <mark>According to the 2005 report by the French Agency for Environmental and Occupational Health Safety (AFSSE), "Evaluation of risks associated with exposure to UV radiation," the risk of skin cancer (carcinoma or melanoma) increases by a factor of 1.10 with 30 tanning sessions per year over a 10-year period, and by 1.39 with 100 sessions.</mark>

<mark>Other exogenous risk factors include arsenic, pesticides, hydrocarbons, tobacco (particularly for SCC of the lower lip), ionizing radiation, and prolonged local chemotherapy.</mark>

## II.1.2. Constitutional Factors

The main constitutional factor is skin phototype, which is genetically determined. Individuals with a poor capacity for tanning are at higher risk.

In xeroderma pigmentosum—a hereditary recessive disorder—deficiency in DNA repair enzymes leads to an inability to correct photoinduced DNA damage, resulting in a markedly increased risk of SCC, actinic keratosis (AK), and keratoacanthoma.

## II.1.3. Other Risk Factors

The following factors contribute to less than 1% of SCC cases: iatrogenic immunosuppression, chronic inflammation, chronic leg ulcers, and scarring.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) infections have been implicated, particularly in genital and anal SCC. HPV is also found in extragenital sites, in both sun-exposed and non-exposed areas, and in both immunocompromised and immunocompetent individuals. However, HPV alone is insufficient to induce malignant transformation. In organ transplant recipients, three synergistic risk factors are present: UV exposure, immunosuppression, and HPV infection.

---

# Key Points

- Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) encompasses a group of malignant primary epithelial skin tumors with malpighian differentiation and is distinct from basal cell carcinoma (BCC).  
- The primary factor promoting the development of SCC, Bowen’s disease (BD), or actinic keratosis (AK) is total lifetime UV exposure, whether from natural sunlight or artificial sources.  
- Skin phototype, a genetically determined trait, influences the risk of developing AK, BD, or SCC.  
- Several co-carcinogens have been identified, some site-specific—such as tobacco for actinic cheilitis and SCC of the lower lip, and HPV for genital or anal SCC.  
- Certain medical conditions predispose to SCC, including chronic inflammation, chronic wounds, and immunosuppression.

---

# II.2. Precursors of SCC

## II.2.1. Actinic Keratosis

### II.2.1.1. Clinical, Histological, Epidemiological Aspects and Natural History

#### Clinical Aspects

Actinic keratosis (AK) consists of common lesions, especially in fair-skinned individuals, occurring in sun-exposed areas such as the face, dorsal aspects of the hands, and scalp in balding individuals. These lesions are often accompanied by other signs of photoaging, such as wrinkles and freckles.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the presence of flat, rough lesions of variable thickness, sometimes more visible than palpable. Lesions typically measure 1 cm or less in diameter and exhibit varying degrees of erythema. They may be pigmented and are often covered with a dry, adherent, yellowish or brownish keratin layer.

In clinical practice, isolated or few AKs are distinguished from multiple AKs, which may coalesce into plaques—particularly on the scalp.

<mark>On the lower lip, actinic cheilitis represents the labial counterpart of AK.</mark> <mark>This condition is uniquely associated with tobacco smoking as a secondary carcinogenic factor and carries a higher risk of metastatic SCC compared to other sites.</mark>

# Squamous Cell Carcinoma Morphologies

<mark>A firm, flesh-colored or erythematous, keratotic papule or plaque is most common (see Fig.</mark> <mark>114-1), but SCCs may also be pigmented.</mark> <mark>Other presentations include an ulcer (Fig.</mark> <mark>114-2), a smooth nodule (Fig.</mark> <mark>114-3), or a thick cutaneous horn.</mark> <mark>SCC may also be verrucous or present as an abscess, particularly if in a periungual location (see Fig.</mark> <mark>113-9 in Chap.</mark> 113). <mark>The margins may be indistinct.</mark> <mark>With enlargement, there is usually increased firmness and elevation.</mark> <mark>Progressive tumor invasion ultimately results in fixation to underlying tissues.</mark> <mark>Especially in the head and neck region, an enlarged lymph node nearby that is firm and non-tender may indicate tumor metastasis (Fig.</mark> 114-4).

# Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

<mark>SCC of the oral cavity usually occurs in patients with a long history of cigarette smoking, tobacco chewing, or alcohol use, but it has now been documented in younger adults without these traditional risk factors.</mark> <mark>There is a male predominance, and the palate and tongue are the most common sites.</mark> <mark>Oral SCC most commonly evolves from lesions of erythroplakia and is usually asymptomatic (see Chap.</mark> 113). <mark>Distinct patterns include a persistent rough red patch or granular velvety red plaque that ultimately becomes firm and nodular.</mark> <mark>Surprisingly, the risk of transformation to SCC does not appear to correlate with the degree of epithelial dysplasia.</mark> <mark>The floor of the mouth, ventrolateral tongue, and soft palate are considered high-risk sites.</mark> <mark>It may also present as a peritonsillar abscess.</mark>

# <mark>Lower Lip Squamous Cell Carcinoma</mark>

<mark>SCC of the lower lip begins as a roughened papule of actinic cheilitis or scaly leukoplakia, with slow progression to a tumor nodule (Fig.</mark> 114-5). <mark>Clinical clues associated with evolving SCC include persistent lip chapping with localized scale or crust, red and white blotchy atrophic vermilion zone of the lip, indistinct or "wandering" vermilion border, and small fissuring or ulceration within an area of indurated actinic cheilitis.</mark>

<mark>Symptoms of underlying pain or altered sensation should be investigated as a potential sign of perineural invasion.</mark>

# Genital Squamous Cell Carcinoma

SCC of the vulva most commonly occurs on the anterior labia majora, beginning as a small warty nodule or an erosive erythematosus plaque.

## <mark>Treatment of Severe Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>

### <mark>High Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** is strongly recommended as monotherapy for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne due to its superior efficacy compared to systemic antibiotics or topical therapy alone.</mark>

### <mark>Medium Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with the fixed-dose combination of **adapalene and benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or with **azelaic acid**, can be recommended for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>

### <mark>Low Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with **adapalene** or **BPO** can be considered for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with systemic antibiotics and topical treatments (excluding topical antibiotics) can be considered.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with a topical treatment (excluding antibiotics) can also be considered.</mark>

### <mark>Open Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>Due to insufficient evidence, no recommendation can be made for or against the use of **intense pulsed light (IPL)** or **laser therapy** in severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>Although **photodynamic therapy (PDT)** shows effectiveness, it cannot currently be recommended due to lack of standardized treatment protocols and concerns about acute adverse reactions.</mark>

### <mark>Negative Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Topical monotherapy** is not recommended for conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral antibiotics** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral anti-androgens** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Artificial UV radiation sources** are not recommended.</mark>
- <mark>**Visible light therapy** as monotherapy is not recommended.</mark>

---

## <mark>Choice of Topical vs. Systemic Treatment</mark>

<mark>There is limited evidence directly comparing topical and systemic therapies or evaluating the added benefit of combination therapy over topical treatment alone.</mark> <mark>Most studies compare topical antibiotic monotherapy with systemic antibiotic monotherapy.</mark>

<mark>In clinical practice, expert consensus supports that:</mark>
- <mark>Patients with **severe papulopustular acne** or **moderate nodular acne** achieve better outcomes with **systemic antibiotic plus topical treatment**, or with **systemic isotretinoin**.</mark>
- <mark>Involvement of the trunk is a key factor favoring systemic therapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic treatments** are associated with better adherence and higher patient satisfaction, particularly in widespread disease.</mark>

---

## <mark>Additional Considerations</mark>

- <mark>**Isotretinoin** is highly effective in severe cases, supported by strong clinical experience despite limited controlled trial data specific to nodular/conglobate forms.</mark>
- <mark>Evidence for many treatment options was downgraded due to reliance on indirect data from studies of severe papulopustular acne, particularly when assessing nodule and cyst reduction.</mark>
- <mark>Prescribers should be mindful of the risk of **antibiotic resistance** when using systemic antibiotics.</mark>
- <mark>Systemic antibiotics such as **doxycycline** and **lymecycline** should be limited to a maximum treatment duration of **3 months**.</mark>
- <mark>In cases where higher-strength recommendations cannot be followed (due to cost, availability, licensing, or legal restrictions), lower-strength alternatives may be used as first-line therapy.</mark>

---

## Treatment of Papulopustular Acne

There is insufficient evidence to recommend laser or light-based therapies (other than blue light) for papulopustular acne due to lack of standardized protocols, clinical trial data, and real-world experience.

Systemic treatment with **isotretinoin** is recommended in severe cases based on high efficacy observed in clinical practice, although safety and tolerability data remain limited and insufficient for guiding recommendations independently.

## Clinical Question 1: For which acne forms is systemic isotretinoin indicated?

### <mark>Summary of Acne Severity and Isotretinoin Indications</mark>

<mark>| Acne Type | Clinical Features | Predominant Lesion Type | Severity |</mark>
<mark>|----------|-------------------|--------------------------|--------|</mark>
<mark>| Comedonal | Predominantly comedones (open and closed) | Comedonal | Mild to moderate |</mark>
<mark>| Mild to moderate papulopustular | Papules and pustules, few comedones | Inflammatory or mixed | Mild to moderate |</mark>
<mark>| Severe papulopustular (may have some nodules) | Widespread papules, pustules, comedones, occasional nodules | Inflammatory/mixed | Severe |</mark>
<mark>| Very severe (nodular/conglobate) | Extensive inflammation, nodules, cysts, scarring | Nodular/conglobate | Very severe |</mark>

**Grading:**
- **4: Severe** – Entire face involved with numerous papules, pustules, comedones, and rare nodules.
- **5: Very Severe** – Highly inflammatory acne with nodules and cysts; may involve face, trunk, or both.

---

### <mark>Indications for Systemic Isotretinoin</mark>

#### <mark>**European Directive (2016 S3 Guidelines)**</mark>
- <mark>**Recommended for:**</mark>
  <mark>- Severe papulopustular acne</mark>
  <mark>- Moderate to severe nodular or conglobate acne</mark>
- <mark>**Strength of Recommendation (SOR):** High</mark>
- <mark>**Positioning:** Second-line therapy after failure of antibiotics and topical treatments</mark>
- <mark>**Important Note:** Oral isotretinoin should only be used in severe, nodular, or conglobate acne that is unresponsive to appropriate topical and systemic therapies.</mark>
- <mark>**Legal Consideration:** Deviating from this guidance may expose prescribers to liability if adverse outcomes occur.</mark>

#### <mark>**Canadian Clinical Practice Guideline (2016)**</mark>
- <mark>**Recommended for:** Severe acne (including cystic/conglobate)</mark>
- <mark>**Strength of Recommendation:** High</mark>
- <mark>**Positioning:** **First-line therapy** in severe, scarring, or refractory acne</mark>
- <mark>**Rationale:** Based on high efficacy, long-term remission rates, safety profile, and patient preference</mark>
- **Definition of High SOR:** Action strongly recommended; definitely use

#### **Expert Consensus and Flexibility**
- <mark>Despite the European directive, many experts support **first-line use** of isotretinoin in:</mark>
  <mark>- Severe, scarring acne</mark>
  <mark>- Acne with significant psychosocial impact</mark>
  <mark>- Acne unresponsive to conventional therapy (refractory)</mark>
  <mark>- Patients at high risk for scarring</mark>
- <mark>**Limitations** (e.g., cost, access, legal or licensing issues) may require use of lower-SOR treatments even when isotretinoin is clinically preferred.</mark>

---

### <mark>Dosing Recommendations</mark>

<mark>|--------|---------------------|---------------------|------------------|</mark>
<mark>| **Daily Dose** | – | 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day | Start ≤0.5 mg/kg/day; increase to 1 mg/kg/day as tolerated |</mark>
<mark>| | | | Often: 0.5 mg/kg for first 4 weeks, then 1 mg/kg |</mark>

<mark>| **Cumulative Dose Target** | – | – | 120–150 mg/kg (associated with lower relapse rates) |</mark>
| **Duration of Treatment** | 16–24 weeks for nodular/conglobate acne | Until full clearance + 1 month | Individualized; typically 16–20 weeks |

---

### <mark>Key Takeaways</mark>

- <mark>**Isotretinoin is indicated for severe, nodular, conglobate, or scarring acne.**</mark>
- <mark>**European guidelines** position it as **second-line** after antibiotic failure.</mark>
- <mark>**Canadian and expert consensus guidelines** support **first-line use** in severe or high-risk cases.</mark>
- <mark>**Dosing:** Start low (≤0.5 mg/kg), escalate to 0.5–1 mg/kg/day; aim for cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg.</mark>
- **Treatment duration:** Continue until complete clearance plus ~1 month, or for at least 16–24 weeks.
- **Clinical judgment, patient factors, and access limitations** influence real-world prescribing.

## <mark>Renal involvement</mark>

<mark>Acute kidney injury associated with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) and accelerated phase hypertension is a serious and potentially fatal complication of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma renal crisis; SRC).</mark> <mark>It most commonly occurs in patients with the progressive, diffuse form of the disease and within the first 4 years of disease onset.</mark> <mark>The presence of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies is a significant risk factor and is detected in approximately one-third of SRC cases.[144]</mark>

<mark>Therefore, regular blood pressure monitoring (at least twice weekly, preferably via home monitoring) is recommended to enable early detection of renal involvement.</mark> <mark>Glucocorticoid use at doses exceeding 15 mg of prednisone equivalents per day should be avoided, as they are associated with an increased risk of renal crisis and have long-term adverse effects.[144]</mark>

<mark>A small subset of patients may develop normotensive renal crisis, often presenting with features of thrombotic microangiopathy.</mark> <mark>Chronic renal involvement in systemic sclerosis is characterized by a slowly progressive obliterative vasculopathy.</mark> <mark>Urinary protein excretion has been identified in multiple studies as a major independent risk factor for mortality.[145] Hence, annual assessment of urinary protein is advised.</mark>

<mark>Consensus criteria for the classification and diagnosis of SRC are currently under development and validation.[146] Additionally, there is a need for improved management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in systemic sclerosis, along with the development of more effective biomarkers and therapeutic strategies.</mark>

## General recommendation for a regular diagnostic work-up in patients with SSc

Following an initial baseline assessment (see Table 6), lifelong follow-up with at least annual evaluations is recommended due to the chronic and potentially progressive nature of systemic sclerosis. Patients with active or progressive disease should be monitored more frequently.

The annual evaluation should include a comprehensive clinical assessment, including modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS), and the following:

- Pulmonary function tests with plethysmography and measurement of diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)
- Blood pressure measurement
- Electrocardiogram
- Echocardiography
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) / C-reactive protein (CRP)
- Complete blood count
- Clinical chemistry (liver function tests, creatinine, urea)
- <mark>Urinary protein assessment</mark>

<mark>In patients at increased risk for renal crisis—such as those with progressive diffuse disease or anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies—frequent blood pressure monitoring is strongly recommended, preferably through home-based measurement (see Table 7).</mark>

## Treatment

### Therapy for skin involvement

### Treatment of Raynaud's phenomenon

Avoidance of cold exposure and consistent protection from cold are essential. Heated gloves, shoes, and hand warmers are commonly used. Additional supportive measures include paraffin baths, heated seed pillows, therapy balls, and physical therapy.

## <mark>Diagnosis and Assessment of Systemic Sclerosis</mark>

### <mark>Disease Characteristics and Risk Factors</mark>
<mark>It occurs most likely in patients with the progressive diffuse form with a disease duration of $< 4$ years.</mark> The presence of **anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies** is considered a particular risk factor and is detected in about one-third of cases.

### Diagnostic Criteria
In 2013, the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) published new classification criteria for systemic sclerosis. However, these criteria were primarily developed for clinical research purposes and cannot be applied to patients without skin involvement of the hands or to those with scleroderma-like disorders.

### Capillaroscopy
Capillaroscopy (e.g., using a nail fold videocapillaroscope, stereomicroscope, or dermatoscope) is a well-established, non-invasive technique for identifying changes in the nail fold capillaries that help differentiate primary Raynaud's phenomenon from systemic sclerosis (SSc).

### Clinical Skin Score
The **modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS)** is the best validated tool for assessing skin sclerosis progression. It is evaluated by manual palpation at 17 different anatomical sites. A score of 0, 1, 2, or 3 is assigned based on the degree of skin thickening:
- 0: Uninvolved skin  
- 1: Mild thickening  
- 2: Moderate thickening  
- 3: Severe thickening  

The total skin score is calculated as the sum of scores across all 17 areas. The mRSS is feasible, reliable, and validated for both initial and follow-up skin evaluation. Proper administration requires experience and adequate training.

### <mark>Laboratory Parameters</mark>
<mark>Autoantibodies targeting specific nuclear antigens are a hallmark of SSc.</mark> <mark>The frequency of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) in SSc patients approaches 95%, consistent with reported rates of 85–99% in the literature.</mark> <mark>In one study, 86.6% of ANA-positive patients had SSc-specific antibodies, with 96.4% recognizing one of five major antigens:</mark>
- <mark>Centromere</mark>  
- <mark>Topoisomerase-1</mark>  
- <mark>RNA polymerase III</mark>  
- <mark>Exosomal ribonucleoprotein (PM/Scl)</mark>  
- <mark>Uridine-rich small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1-snRNP)</mark>  

<mark>These SSc-specific autoantibodies are generally mutually exclusive; co-occurrence in individual patients is rare.</mark>

### Organ-Oriented Diagnostic Workup
A comprehensive baseline assessment—including clinical, laboratory, and radiographic evaluations—is essential to determine the patient’s overall condition and organ involvement. Recommended diagnostic procedures are summarized in relevant guidelines. Lifelong follow-up is advised at least annually due to the chronic nature of the disease. In patients with progressive disease activity, more frequent monitoring is warranted.

# <mark>Differential Diagnoses</mark>

<mark>Localized scleroderma (LS), scleromyxedema, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, scleredema, and systemic sclerosis (SSc) overlap syndromes should be considered in the differential diagnosis.</mark> <mark>To differentiate primary from secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, nail fold capillaroscopy and autoantibody analysis are essential.</mark> Secondary causes such as vasculitis, thromboangiitis obliterans, or arteriosclerotic vascular disease should be excluded—evaluation may include tests such as the Allen test or fist closure test. Calcinosis cutis lesions must be distinguished from superficial ulcerations, although they may predispose to digital ulcers. Muscle biopsy can help determine the histological and ultrastructural features of myositis when present.

# Treatment

<mark>Tailoring treatment to the individual patient requires accurate assessment of disease subset, organ involvement, and disease activity.</mark> <mark>In recent years, an organ-based approach has led to significant pharmacologic advancements, substantially improving prognosis and quality of life for specific patient subgroups.</mark>

# Physical examination

## General assessment

It is recommended to evaluate the following aspects:

- <mark>**Extent of skin and mucous membrane lesions**, including the degree of mucosal damage and associated functional impairments such as dysphagia, dysphonia, weight loss, visual disturbances, and dyspareunia.</mark>
- **Disease activity quantification** using one of the two validated scoring systems: the **Pemphigus Disease Area Index (PDAI)** or the **Autoimmune Bullous Skin Intensity and Severity Score (ABSIS)** $(4.5 \pm 1.0)$.

Assessment of the patient’s general condition and co-morbidities should include:

- Body weight
- Arterial blood pressure
- Presence of co-morbidities (e.g., neoplastic, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, diabetes)

The use of **DLQI**, and/or the **ABQOL** and **TABQOL** questionnaires—specific for autoimmune bullous diseases—may be considered $(4.2 \pm 1.2)$.

Check vaccination status. Inquire about potential travel to countries where live vaccination is required; if so, ensure such vaccinations are completed before initiating immunosuppressive therapy.

The classical **Nikolsky's sign** is generally not recommended by most experts, as it may induce new lesions in already compromised skin and is not necessary for assessing disease activity given the availability of validated scoring tools.

## <mark>Clinical subtypes</mark>

### <mark>Pemphigus vulgaris (PV)</mark>

- <mark>Typically presents with **oral mucosal lesions**: painful, persistent erosions of the buccal mucosa and/or gingiva that interfere with eating.</mark>
- <mark>Less commonly, non-cicatricial lesions may affect the eyes, nose, larynx, esophagus, genitals, and anus.</mark>
- <mark>**Cutaneous involvement** may appear weeks to months after mucosal lesions.</mark>
  <mark>- Characterized by **flaccid bullae** with clear content, arising on non-erythematous skin, rapidly evolving into erosions.</mark>
  <mark>- Lesions may be localized or generalized, commonly affecting seborrhoeic areas (face, scalp, chest, interscapular region) and mechanically stressed areas, including extremities.</mark>
  <mark>- The disease is usually **not associated with significant pruritus**.</mark>
  <mark>- **Fingernail involvement** can occur.</mark>

### <mark>Pemphigus foliaceus (PF)</mark>

- <mark>Presents with **cutaneous involvement only**; **no mucosal lesions**.</mark>
- <mark>Features transient, **flaccid bullae** or superficial, "puff pastry-like" exfoliation that progresses to crusted erosions.</mark>
- <mark>Predilection for **seborrhoeic areas**: scalp, face, chest, and interscapular region.</mark>
- <mark>More extensive disease is seen in sporadic and endemic forms (e.g., *Fogo Selvagem*, Brazilian pemphigus, Tunisian pemphigus).</mark>

### <mark>Paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP)</mark>

- <mark>Should be suspected in patients with an associated malignancy, particularly **non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma**, **chronic lymphocytic leukemia**, **thymoma**, or **Castleman’s disease**.</mark>
- <mark>The underlying tumor may not yet be diagnosed at the time of PNP presentation, and **PNP symptoms may precede malignancy detection**.</mark>

#### <mark>Mucosal involvement:</mark>
- <mark>Initial manifestations include **cheilitis** and/or **ulcerative stomatitis**, with persistent painful erosions leading to **severe dysphagia**.</mark>
- <mark>**Cicatricial conjunctivitis**, **keratitis**, and **genital involvement** are common.</mark>
- <mark>**Pharyngeal**, **nasal**, and **esophageal** involvement may occur, resulting in **phagodynia**.</mark>

#### <mark>Cutaneous involvement:</mark>
- <mark>**Polymorphic skin lesions** resembling:</mark>
  <mark>- Lichen planus</mark>
  <mark>- Graft-versus-host disease</mark>
  <mark>- Erythema multiforme</mark>
  <mark>- Bullous pemphigoid</mark>
  <mark>- Pemphigus vulgaris</mark>
- <mark>**Palmar involvement** is frequent.</mark>

#### <mark>Pulmonary involvement:</mark>
- <mark>A **characteristic and life-threatening complication**, including:</mark>
  <mark>- Alveolitis</mark>
  <mark>- Bronchiolitis obliterans</mark>
  <mark>- Pulmonary fibrosis</mark>

# Major objectives

- <mark>To confirm the clinical diagnosis of **pemphigus**.</mark>
- <mark>To identify risk factors, severity factors, and potential comorbidities through detailed history and initial clinical evaluation.</mark>
- <mark>To determine the type of initial involvement (skin, mucosa) and assess its extent.</mark>
- <mark>To evaluate prognosis based on patient age and overall general health.</mark>
- <mark>To measure the extent and distribution of lesions using validated scoring systems: **Autoimmune Bullous Skin Intensity and Severity Score (ABSIS)** or **Pemphigus Disease Area Index (PDAI)**.</mark>
- <mark>To assess the impact on quality of life using dermatology-specific tools such as **DLQI (Dermatology Life Quality Index)** and autoimmune blistering disease-specific instruments (**ABQOL**, **TABQOL**).</mark>
- <mark>To initiate prompt treatment aimed at achieving disease control and complete remission as early as possible.</mark>

# Professions involved

The management of pemphigus should be led by an experienced **dermatologist**, typically based in a tertiary referral center, specialized clinic, or within a recognized expert network.

Supportive roles may be provided by the following healthcare professionals:

- Consultant dermatologist in general practice  
- The patient’s general practitioner  
- Specialists relevant to the patient’s condition and comorbidities, including:
  - Internists
  - Cardiologists
  - Stomatologists
  - Ophthalmologists
  - Otorhinolaryngologists
  - Gastroenterologists
  - Gynaecologists
  - Urologists
  - Proctologists
  - Rheumatologists
  - Oncologists
  - Psychologists  
- Health nurses, particularly for home care in elderly or disabled patients with residual mucosal or skin lesions post-hospitalization  
- Dietician and physiotherapist  
- Nurse specialist/practitioner  

It is recommended that:

- A dermatologist with expertise in pemphigus oversees the initial treatment plan.
- Other healthcare professionals are integrated into the care team based on disease involvement, severity, comorbidities, and complications.

# <mark>Clinical examination</mark>

## Medical history

It is recommended to document the following:

- Time of first onset of symptoms.
- Functional symptoms: pain, pruritus, severity of dysphagia, ocular and ENT symptoms, dysuria, anogenital discomfort, and weight loss.
- Past medical history related to haematological, oncologic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and infectious conditions — to identify risks associated with **oral corticosteroid use** and potential complications of **immunosuppressive therapy**.
- Assessment of pregnancy potential and current contraceptive practices, especially if immunosuppressive therapy is planned.
- Review of recent medication use that may induce pemphigus, including:
  - ACE inhibitors
  - Angiotensin receptor blockers
  - Beta-blockers
  - Cephalosporins
  - Phenylbutazone
  - Pyritinol
  - Thiopronine
  - Rifampicin  
  *(Note: D-penicillamine, a classic cause of drug-induced pemphigus, is now rarely used.)*  
  Consider discontinuation of suspected drugs if there is a clear temporal relationship between drug initiation and lesion onset.

- Evaluation of quality-of-life impact using validated questionnaires such as **DLQI**, **ABQOL**, or **TABQOL**.

- Verification of vaccination status. Inquire about planned travel to regions requiring live vaccines — these should be administered **before** starting immunosuppressive therapy.

# Physical examination

## General examination

It is recommended to assess:

- Extent of skin and mucous membrane involvement.
- Degree of mucosal damage and associated functional impairments:
  - Dysphagia
  - Dysphonia
  - Weight loss
  - Visual disturbances
  - Dyspareunia

It is recommended to quantify skin and mucosal lesion burden using one of the two validated scoring systems:  
**Pemphigus Disease Area Index (PDAI)** or **Autoimmune Bullous Skin Intensity and Severity Score (ABSIS)**.

# MUCOUS MEMBRANES

<mark>In the majority of patients, painful mucous membrane erosions are the presenting sign of pemphigus vulgaris (PV) and may be the only sign for an average of 5 months before skin lesions develop.</mark> <mark>However, the presenting symptoms may vary according to geographic area.</mark> <mark>For example, in a study from Croatia, painful oral lesions were the presenting symptom in only 32 percent of patients.</mark> <mark>Most of these patients progressed to a more generalized eruption within 5 months to 1 year; however, some had oral lesions for more than 5 years before generalization.</mark> <mark>On the other hand, in Tehran, 62 percent of patients presented with oral lesions.</mark>

<mark>The mucous membranes most often affected are those of the oral cavity, which is involved in almost all patients with PV and is often the only mucous membrane involved.</mark> <mark>Intact blisters are rare, likely due to their fragility and tendency to rupture easily.</mark> <mark>Scattered and often extensive erosions may appear on any part of the oral cavity, although they occur most frequently on the buccal mucosa.</mark> <mark>These erosions may spread to involve the pharynx and larynx, leading to hoarseness.</mark> <mark>Often, these erosions are so painful that the patient is unable to eat or drink adequately.</mark>

<mark>Mucous membranes in other areas may also be affected by painful erosions, including the nasal mucosa, conjunctiva, anus, penis, vagina, labia, and, in rare cases, the esophagus.</mark>

<mark>Skin involvement without mucous membrane involvement in PV is unusual and was reported in only 11 percent of cases in one study.</mark>

## SKIN

The characteristic clinical lesions of pemphigus foliaceus (PF) are scaly, crusted erosions, often on an erythematous base. In more localized and early disease, these lesions are typically well demarcated and distributed in a seborrheic pattern, affecting the face, scalp, and upper trunk.

## Types of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)

### <mark>Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
<mark>In acquired (type I) PCT, uroporphyrinogen (UROGEN) decarboxylase deficiency is restricted to the liver.</mark> <mark>This tissue-specific deficiency may result from either a liver-specific gene defect or exposure to chemicals that selectively inhibit the hepatic form of the enzyme without affecting the erythrocyte (RBC) enzyme.</mark> <mark>Certain substances trigger PCT only in susceptible individuals—such as **alcohol** and **estrogens**—while others, like **hexachlorobenzene (HCB)**, can induce the disease in nearly all exposed individuals.</mark>

### Hereditary (Type II) PCT
Hereditary (type II) PCT is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by approximately 50% reduction in UROGEN decarboxylase activity across all tissues, including RBCs and cultured skin fibroblasts. Enzyme levels show a bimodal distribution:
- A large group (>80%) has normal enzyme concentration.
- A smaller group (<20%) exhibits about half the normal amount of detectable enzyme.

Some patients with type II PCT have enzyme activity at the lower end of the normal range. Clinical penetrance is low (~20%), indicating that most individuals with the genetic defect do not develop symptoms. This implies that additional genetic or environmental factors are required for disease expression. Over 100 mutations in the *UROGEN decarboxylase* gene have been identified, many of which impair enzyme stability or cause defective pre-mRNA splicing.

### Type III PCT
Not all patients with a family history of PCT have type II disease. Some individuals have multiple affected relatives but normal RBC UROGEN decarboxylase activity. This variant has been termed **type III PCT** by some researchers. Possible explanations include:
- Inheritance of a UROGEN decarboxylase variant that appears normal immunologically but is selectively vulnerable to hepatic inhibition.
- Presence of a second inherited enzyme defect unrelated to UROGEN decarboxylase.

These hypotheses remain under investigation.

### Differential Diagnosis and Dual Porphyrias
Some cases originally classified as hereditary PCT may actually represent **variegate porphyria (VP)**, another autosomal dominant porphyria. Families with both PCT and VP have been described ("dual porphyrias"). Additionally, coexistence of PCT and **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)** has been reported, further complicating diagnosis and classification.

## <mark>Precipitating Factors in Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
Multiple agents and conditions are associated with the development of sporadic (type I) PCT:

- <mark>**Alcohol**</mark>
- <mark>**Estrogenic hormones**</mark>
- <mark>**Iron overload**</mark>
- <mark>**Viral infections** (hepatitis C, HIV)</mark>
- <mark>**Polychlorinated hydrocarbons** (e.g., HCB, TCDD)</mark>
- **Hemodialysis** in renal failure

### Alcohol
<mark>Alcohol consumption is a well-established trigger for PCT.</mark> <mark>Ethanol induces hepatic **ALA synthase**, the rate-limiting enzyme in heme synthesis.</mark> <mark>It also reduces erythrocyte UROGEN decarboxylase activity in both acute and chronic alcohol use.</mark> <mark>Ethanol inhibits other heme pathway enzymes, including **ferrochelatase** and **ALA dehydratase**.</mark> <mark>Chronic alcoholism suppresses erythropoiesis and increases intestinal iron absorption, effects potentially amplified by mutations linked to **hemochromatosis**.</mark>

## Candidal and Dermatophyte Nail Involvement

Candidal onychomycosis is characterized by invasion of pseudohyphae throughout the entire nail plate, adjacent cuticle, granular layer, and stratum spinosum of the nail bed, as well as the hyponychial stratum corneum. In contrast, dermatophyte infections show a predilection for the ventral nail and nail bed stratum corneum. Histopathologically, the epidermis may exhibit spongiosis and focal parakeratosis, with minimal dermal inflammatory response. In white superficial onychomycosis (WSO), organisms are confined to the dorsal nail surface and display distinctive "perforating organs" and "eroding fronds."

---

## Treatment of Dermatophytes

### <mark>Tinea Capitis/Favus</mark>

<mark>Multiple systemic and topical antifungal agents are effective against dermatophytes.</mark> <mark>Infections involving hair-bearing skin require oral therapy due to fungal invasion of the hair follicle.</mark>

#### <mark>Griseofulvin</mark>
<mark>Griseofulvin remains the only oral antifungal approved by the U.S.</mark> <mark>Food and Drug Administration for tinea capitis.</mark> <mark>The traditional pediatric dose was 10–20 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks, administered with a fatty meal to enhance absorption.</mark> <mark>However, due to reported high failure rates, current expert recommendations favor higher doses: 20–25 mg/kg/day of the microsize formulation or 15 mg/kg/day of the ultramicrosize formulation, given for 8 weeks—though this is not based on controlled clinical trials.</mark>

<mark>Disadvantages include poor compliance due to treatment duration and cost, bitter taste in liquid form, photosensitivity, headache, and gastrointestinal side effects.</mark> <mark>Griseofulvin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P₄₅₀ enzymes.</mark> <mark>Routine laboratory monitoring is not required for standard treatment courses.</mark>

#### Fluconazole
<mark>Available in both tablet and palatable liquid forms, fluconazole at 6 mg/kg/day for 20 days achieves an 89% cure rate in *Trichophyton tonsurans* tinea capitis.</mark> <mark>Alternative regimens include weekly dosing of 8 mg/kg for 8–16 weeks or 6 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks, followed by a single week of retreatment 4 weeks later if clinically indicated.</mark>

Fluconazole absorption is unaffected by food, and gastrointestinal side effects are uncommon. Hepatotoxicity has been reported but is less frequent than with ketoconazole.

#### Itraconazole
At doses of 3–5 mg/kg/day, itraconazole effectively clears tinea capitis caused by *Microsporum* or *Trichophyton* species within 4–6 weeks. Pulse therapy (5 mg/kg/day for 1 week per month, repeated for 1–3 cycles) is also effective.

Adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea (particularly with the liquid formulation), and peripheral edema—especially when co-administered with calcium channel blockers. Hepatotoxicity is rare compared to ketoconazole, though cases of hepatic failure have been reported. Rare associations with congestive heart failure exist.

#### Terbinafine
Terbinafine at 3–6 mg/kg/day cures *Trichophyton* tinea capitis in 2–4 weeks, but 4–8 weeks are needed for *Microsporum* infections. A randomized trial comparing 4 weeks of terbinafine to 8 weeks of griseofulvin showed no overall significant difference in efficacy. However, subgroup analysis revealed superior response to terbinafine in *Trichophyton* infections, whereas *M. audouinii* infections responded better to griseofulvin.

# <mark>Oral Antifungals</mark>

<mark>Oral antifungals are reserved for widespread or more inflammatory lesions.</mark> <mark>Comparative studies in adults show that fluconazole, 150 mg weekly for 4 to 6 weeks; itraconazole, 100 mg daily for 15 days; and terbinafine, 250 mg daily for 2 weeks are as effective as griseofulvin, 500 mg daily for 2 to 6 weeks, with no significant differences in adverse events.</mark> <mark>Safe and effective regimens for children include ultramicrosize griseofulvin, 10 to 20 mg/kg/day for up to 6 weeks; itraconazole, 5 mg/kg/day for 1 week; and terbinafine, 3 to 6 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks.</mark>

# Tinea Pedis

Mild interdigital tinea pedis without bacterial involvement can be treated topically with an allylamine, azole, ciclopirox, benzylamine, tolnaftate, or undecenoic acid. Topical terbinafine for 1 week is 66% effective.

The newer oral antifungals have replaced griseofulvin as the treatments of choice for severe or refractory tinea pedis, especially when accompanied by onychomycosis. The recommended dosing schedule for terbinafine is 250 mg daily for 2 weeks. Effective regimens for itraconazole in adults include 200 mg twice daily for 1 week, 200 mg daily for 3 weeks, or 100 mg daily for 4 weeks, whereas children should receive 5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks. Fluconazole, 150 mg weekly for 3 to 4 weeks or 50 mg daily for 30 days, is also effective. Associated onychomycosis is common; if present, treatment of the nail infection is necessary to prevent recurrence of tinea pedis.

Maceration, denudation, pruritus, and malodor warrant evaluation for bacterial co-infection via Gram stain and culture. Antibiotics should be initiated once bacterial infection is confirmed and selected based on sensitivity results.

Vesiculobullous tinea pedis results from a T-cell-mediated immune reaction; therefore, symptomatic relief with topical or systemic corticosteroids may be appropriate at the onset of antifungal therapy.

# Onychomycosis

Treatment of onychomycosis depends on the severity of nail involvement and the causative organism. Onychomycosis can be categorized based on whether the matrix is involved. In cases without matrix involvement, topical therapy alone may be sufficient. However, oral or combination therapy is recommended for cases with matrix involvement.

Ciclopirox (8% nail lacquer) is a topical agent that can be effective for tinea unguium, applied daily for 48 weeks. In mild to moderate disease, it achieves mycologic cure and clear nails in approximately 7% of cases. It also has activity against *Candida* species and some molds. Despite its lower efficacy compared to oral antifungals, ciclopirox avoids risks of systemic drug interactions, making it a consideration for long-term use in older patients.

Amorolfine is another topical agent formulated as a nail lacquer and belongs to the morpholine derivative class. It is effective against dermatophytes, yeasts, and molds and can be applied once weekly.

Oral antifungals are indicated for refractory, severe, or nondermatophyte onychomycosis, or when a shorter treatment duration or higher cure rate is desired. Selection of an agent should be guided by the causative organism, potential adverse effects, and risk of drug interactions.

Terbinafine is fungicidal against dermatophytes, *Aspergillus*, and *Scopulariopsis*, but has variable activity against *Candida* species.

## Skin Manifestations of Onchocerciasis

<mark>Skin involvement in onchocerciasis can present in various forms, including **acute papular onchodermatitis**, **chronic papular onchodermatitis**, **lichenified onchodermatitis**, **atrophy**, and **depigmentation**.</mark> <mark>Palpable onchocercal nodules may also be present.</mark> <mark>More than one pattern of skin involvement may occur simultaneously, or one pattern may evolve into another over time.</mark>

<mark>**Pruritus** is often the first symptom of infection.</mark> 

### Acute Papular Onchodermatitis
- <mark>Typically affects the **face**, **extremities**, and **trunk**</mark>
- Characterized by widespread **small pruritic papules**, **vesicles**, and **pustules**
- May be accompanied by **erythema** and **edema**
- A similar rash can be precipitated by treatment with **ivermectin** or **diethylcarbamazine (DEC)** in infected individuals

### <mark>Chronic Papular Onchodermatitis</mark>
- <mark>Lesions consist of **macules** and **lichenoid papules**, 3–9 mm in diameter</mark>
- <mark>**Pruritus** is common</mark>
- <mark>**Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** may develop</mark>
- <mark>Most frequently involves the **buttocks**, **shoulders**, and **waist**</mark>

### <mark>Other Skin Changes</mark>
- **Lichenified onchodermatitis**: results from chronic scratching and rubbing
- **Atrophy**: resembles age-related skin atrophy
- **Depigmentation**: may mimic post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or vitiligo

## <mark>Related Physical Findings</mark>

<mark>**Palpable onchocercal nodules**:</mark>
- <mark>Contain adult worms within the **deep dermis** and **subcutaneous tissue**</mark>
- <mark>Typically **asymptomatic**</mark>
- <mark>Located over bony prominences such as the **skull**, **iliac crest**, **knee**, **ribs**, **sacrum**, **scapula**, and **trochanter**</mark>

## <mark>Laboratory Tests</mark>

- **Peripheral eosinophilia** is common
- **Elevated serum IgE levels** are frequently observed

## <mark>Special Tests</mark>

- <mark>Diagnosis is most commonly confirmed by:</mark>
  <mark>- Identification of **microfilariae** in a **skin snip**</mark>
  <mark>- Visualization of an **adult worm** in an excised nodule</mark>
- **Slit-lamp examination** of the eye may reveal microfilariae in the **anterior chamber**
- <mark>**Antibody testing** lacks specificity</mark>
- **PCR testing** is available primarily through research laboratories

## <mark>Differential Diagnosis</mark>

The differential diagnosis varies based on clinical presentation:

- **Pruritus alone**: consider **scabies**
- **Acute papular onchodermatitis**: may resemble **miliaria**, **insect bites**, or **eczema**
- **Chronic papular onchodermatitis**: can mimic **chronic eczema**, **lichenoid dermatitis**, or **atopic dermatitis**
- **Lichenified onchodermatitis**: differential includes any condition causing chronic pruritus or friction (e.g., lichen simplex chronicus)
- **Skin atrophy**: consider normal aging or other causes of dermal atrophy
- **Depigmentation**: differentiate from post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or **vitiligo**
- **Onchocercal nodules**: consider other parasitic nodules (e.g., cysticercosis) or **epidermal inclusion cysts**

## Treatment

> **Ivermectin** is the drug of choice for onchocerciasis.

- **Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)** should **not** be used in confirmed cases due to:
  - Lack of efficacy against adult worms
  - Risk of severe **ocular reactions**

- **Mazzotti test** (diagnostic use of DEC):
  - A single **50-mg dose of DEC** may be used in areas where **loiasis is not endemic**
  - In infected individuals, it provokes a reaction within hours:
    - Worsening of cutaneous symptoms
    - Migration of microfilariae to the dermis
    - Allows confirmation via skin biopsy

Ivermectin effectively reduces microfilarial load and prevents disease progression, though it does not reliably kill adult worms.

# <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

## <mark>SUPERFICIAL STAPHYLOCOCCAL PYODERMAS</mark>

<mark>Pyodermas are infections of the epidermis, just below the stratum corneum, or in hair follicles.</mark> In industrialized nations, *S. <mark>aureus* is the most common cause of superficial pyodermas.</mark> However, group A streptococcus remains a frequent cause of pyoderma in developing countries. If left untreated, these infections can extend into the dermis, leading to complications such as ecthyma and furuncle formation.

### <mark>Impetigo</mark>

Two clinical forms of impetigo are recognized: bullous and non-bullous.

- <mark>**Bullous impetigo** is caused exclusively by *S. aureus*.</mark>
- <mark>**Non-bullous impetigo** is most commonly caused by *S. aureus* in industrialized nations, with group A streptococcus being a less frequent cause. In developing countries, group A streptococcus remains a common etiologic agent of non-bullous impetigo.</mark>

## <mark>Superantigens and Immune Evasion in *S. aureus*</mark>

<mark>Although conventional antigens require recognition by all five elements of the T-cell-receptor complex, superantigens bind directly to the variable region of the β chain of the T-cell receptor.</mark> <mark>This unique interaction bypasses normal antigen processing and presentation, leading to the activation of 5% to 30% of resting T cells.</mark> In contrast, a typical antigenic response activates only 0.0001% to 0.01% of T cells.

Non-specific T-cell activation results in a massive systemic release of cytokines, including:
- **Interleukin-2 (IL-2)**
- **Interferon-γ (IFN-γ)**
- **Tumor necrosis factor-β (TNF-β)** from T cells  
- **Interleukin-1 (IL-1)** and **tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)** from macrophages

Superantigens also drive the expansion of lymphocytes expressing specific T-cell-receptor variable regions of the β chain. They can activate B cells, potentially leading to elevated levels of **immunoglobulin E (IgE)** or production of **autoantibodies**. Additionally, superantigens have been shown to selectively induce **cutaneous lymphocyte-associated antigen (CLA)** on T cells, directing their migration ("homing") to the skin.

## <mark>Immune Evasion Mechanisms of *S. aureus*</mark>

*S. <mark>aureus* employs multiple strategies to evade immune clearance:</mark>
- <mark>Approximately 60% of strains secrete **chemotaxis inhibitory protein of staphylococci (CHIPS)**, which blocks neutrophil chemotaxis.</mark>
- <mark>**Protein A** binds the Fc region of IgG, preventing opsonization.</mark>
- <mark>**Staphylokinase** promotes fibrinolysis and interferes with phagocytosis.</mark>
- <mark>**Capsular polysaccharide**, **fibrinogen-binding protein**, and **clumping factor A** help resist opsonophagocytosis.</mark>
- <mark>**Staphylokinase** and **aureolysin** bind and cleave antimicrobial peptides, enhancing bacterial survival both in vitro and likely in vivo.</mark>

## <mark>Drug Resistance in *S. aureus*</mark>

Antibiotic resistance is a major challenge in managing staphylococcal infections. The widespread use of penicillins has led to the emergence of **methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA)**, a significant epidemiological concern since the 1980s. Methicillin resistance confers **pan-resistance to all β-lactam antibiotics**.

More recently, **intermediate-level resistance to vancomycin (VISA)** has emerged, posing an additional therapeutic threat. While overall *S. aureus* infection rates remain stable, the proportion of MRSA isolates has increased in several countries.

High-risk groups for MRSA colonization or infection include:
- Adults over 65 years
- Chronically ill individuals
- Patients with prolonged hospital stays (especially post-surgery)
- Exposure to MRSA-positive individuals
- Prior antibiotic use

The primary reservoirs for MRSA are **healthcare workers** and **hospitalized patients**, with transmission occurring mainly via direct contact.

Efforts to eradicate MRSA have largely failed. Topical **mupirocin** applied to the anterior nares and wounds reduces *S. aureus* colonization, but studies show it may not prevent transmission—for example, in long-term care facilities. Although mupirocin is effective in decolonization, its indiscriminate use should be avoided due to the rising incidence of **mupirocin-resistant strains**.

## Immunity Against *S. aureus*

The primary defense against *S. aureus* is **innate immunity**, particularly mediated by **neutrophils**. A key component of this response is **antimicrobial peptides**, such as:
- Dermicidin
- LL-37
- Protegrin
- α-defensins and β-defensins
- Lactoferricin
- Cascocidin

Despite the presence of circulating antibodies to staphylococcal cell-wall antigens and extracellular toxins in most adults—indicating frequent exposure—these antibodies are **not sufficient for protective immunity**.

Emerging evidence shows that *S. aureus* can **invade and survive within host cells**, including epithelial and immune cells. This intracellular persistence suggests that **cell-mediated immunity** is essential for clearing the infection.

---

## Clinical Findings

### Superficial Staphylococcal Pyodermas

Pyodermas are infections localized to the epidermis, just beneath the stratum corneum, or within hair follicles.

<mark>Lateral resection margins for primary cutaneous melanoma should be determined based on the depth of tumor infiltration, as follows:</mark>

- <mark>**In situ melanoma**: 0.5 cm margin</mark>  
- <mark>**0.1–1 mm melanoma**: 1 cm margin</mark>  
- <mark>**1.1–2 mm melanoma**: 1–2 cm margin</mark>  
- <mark>**>2 mm melanoma**: 2 cm margin</mark>  

<mark>(Recommendation Grade B)</mark>

<mark>No robust evidence is available regarding optimal resection depth.</mark> <mark>Therefore, the project team recommends resection down to the fascia, while preserving the fascia when possible.</mark>  
<mark>(Recommendation Grade C)</mark>

# For cases of Dubreuilh melanoma or lentigo maligna melanoma

The project team supports maintaining the 2005 guidelines for surgical management of in situ lentigo maligna-type melanomas. Data on imiquimod (which lacks marketing authorization for this indication) and radiotherapy are insufficient to establish definitive clinical guidelines for routine use. However, in rare cases of inoperable melanoma, these treatments may be considered on a case-by-case basis, preferably within clinical trials.

## <mark>Recommendation</mark>

- A **1 cm margin** is recommended for Dubreuilh melanomas.  
- If a 1 cm margin is not feasible for anatomical or functional reasons, a **0.5 cm margin** may be accepted, provided that strict histological margin control is performed using techniques such as Mohs surgery or equivalent methods with intraoperative margin assessment, or via a two-stage surgical approach. (Expert opinion)

- In very rare cases of inoperable melanoma, **radiotherapy or imiquimod** (off-label use) may be considered following multidisciplinary team (MCM) discussion. (Expert opinion)

# Topic 3: Sentinel lymph node biopsy

<mark>The available literature primarily focuses on intermediate and final results from the MSLT1 study.</mark>

<mark>Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) allows accurate staging and is a strong independent prognostic factor for melanoma.</mark> <mark>However, it has not been shown to improve overall survival.</mark> <mark>Therefore, it cannot be considered standard treatment.</mark> <mark>It may be offered for melanomas >1 mm in thickness, provided the patient is fully informed about the lack of proven therapeutic benefit.</mark> <mark>SLNB should only be performed in centers with established expertise in the technique.</mark>

## Recommendation

- <mark>**SLNB is an option** for melanomas >1 mm thick. If performed, it must be carried out in a center with adequate expertise.</mark>  
- <mark>**SLNB is not recommended** for melanomas <1 mm thick. (Recommendation Grade A)</mark>  
- <mark>SLNB may also be considered within clinical trials, particularly in the context of adjuvant therapy. (Expert opinion)</mark>

# Role of lymph node dissection

When sentinel lymph node biopsy is not performed, published data on systematic lymph node dissection have not evolved since the 2005 recommendations, which remain valid.

For cases where SLNB is performed, current evidence does not definitively support whether immediate completion lymph node dissection (CLND) after a positive SLNB improves outcomes. Until results from the MSLT2 study are available, no evidence-based recommendation can be made. In France, the prevailing practice is to perform immediate CLND upon detection of a positive sentinel node, although this approach lacks strong supporting evidence.

## Recommendation

- **Systematic lymph node dissection is not recommended** in Stage I–II melanomas when SLNB has not been performed. (Evidence Level A)  
- When SLNB is positive, there is no conclusive evidence to favor immediate dissection over delayed dissection at clinical relapse. The project team endorses continuing the current common practice of **immediate lymph node dissection** in such cases. (Expert opinion)

# Topic 4: Adjuvant treatments

## Medical treatments

Currently, **interferon** is the only medical treatment considered for adjuvant therapy in high-risk melanoma. However, its impact on overall survival remains uncertain, leading to variable international recommendations ranging from "not recommended" to "recommended."

Other agents evaluated—such as gangliosides, **ipilimumab**, and **bevacizumab**—have not demonstrated proven efficacy in improving overall survival and are not authorized for use in melanoma. Therefore, they cannot be recommended for routine clinical use.

# <mark>Recommendation</mark>

Time should be allowed to clearly explain the objectives to the patient, including therapeutic education, sun protection, and self-monitoring, at the time of diagnosis.

---

## Initial Diagnostic Evaluation by Stage

### Stages IA and IB

- Full clinical examination, particularly of the entire skin (integument) and lymph nodes.
- No systematic additional investigations are recommended.  
**(Expert opinion)**

---

### Stages IIA and IIB

- Full clinical examination, including complete skin and lymph node assessment.
- Ultrasound imaging of the regional lymphatic drainage basins.

> While ultrasound has higher sensitivity than clinical examination alone for detecting lymph node metastases, no study has demonstrated a survival benefit from its use.

**(Expert opinion)**

---

### Stages IIC and IIIA

- Full clinical examination of the skin and lymph nodes.
- Ultrasound imaging of the lymphatic drainage system (recommended for Stage IIC).
- Optional imaging with cerebral and thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT (C-TAP CT) or $^{18}$F-FDG-PET:

> Although $^{18}$F-FDG-PET appears more sensitive than CT, no formal recommendation favoring one over the other can be made due to variable availability.

**(Expert opinion)**

---

### Stages IIIB and IIIC

**(Expert opinion)**

## Immunohistochemistry Prognostic Markers in Melanoma

- There is no indication for the systematic use of immunohistochemical prognostic markers in stages I–III.  
**(Recommendation Grade A)**

---

## Role of Oncogenetic Consultation in Melanoma Management

An oncogenetic consultation is recommended in the following situations:

- At least two invasive melanomas in first- or second-degree relatives or in the same individual, diagnosed before age 75.
- Personal or family history of invasive cutaneous or ocular melanoma associated with:
  - Pancreatic cancer
  - Kidney cancer
  - Mesothelioma
  - Central nervous system tumor

> Genes currently associated with melanoma risk include:
> - High-risk: *CDKN2A*, *CDK4*, *BAP1*
> - Intermediate susceptibility: *MC1R*, *MITF*

*(Reference to French guidelines acknowledged; no additional literature review performed by this group)*

---

## Topic 5B: Follow-up

### Stages IA and IB

- 5-year recurrence risk:
  - Stage IA: 1% to 7.1%
  - Stage IB: 1% to 18%
- Types of recurrence (in decreasing frequency):
  - Local or in-transit cutaneous
  - Lymphatic
  - Distant
- Recurrences may occur after short or very long intervals — occasionally more than 10 years post-diagnosis.

# Topic 1: Classification

To standardize melanoma staging and improve communication among multidisciplinary teams, the 7th edition of the **American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)** classification was adopted as the most appropriate system. This classification is based on robust methodological development and offers a widely accepted, practical framework for clinical use.

Key changes introduced in the 7th edition compared to previous versions include:

- **Clark’s level of invasion** is no longer recommended for routine use.  
- For melanomas **< 1 mm in thickness**, the **mitotic rate** has replaced Clark’s level as a prognostic factor.  
- **Lymph node micrometastases** detected by **immunohistochemistry (IHC)** are now included in the **N1 category**, reflecting their clinical significance.

## <mark>Recommendation</mark>

- The **7th edition of the AJCC melanoma classification** is recommended for staging patients with cutaneous melanoma.  
  **(Evidence Level A)**

This classification system is detailed in Annex 1 of the original report.

---

# <mark>Topic 2: Resection Margins</mark>

Evidence from one randomized controlled trial and three meta-analyses has not demonstrated a clear survival benefit for wider resection margins over more conservative ones. However, most international guidelines (with the exception of those from the United Kingdom) recommend that resection margins should not exceed **2 cm**.

## Recommendation

<mark>Lateral resection margins for **primary cutaneous melanoma** should be determined according to **tumor thickness**, as follows:</mark>

- <mark>**Melanoma in situ**: **0.5 cm** margin</mark>  
- <mark>**Melanoma 0.1–1.0 mm thick**: **1 cm** margin</mark>  
- <mark>**Melanoma 1.1–2.0 mm thick**: **1–2 cm** margin</mark>  
- <mark>**Melanoma >2.0 mm thick**: **2 cm** margin</mark>  

<mark>**(Recommendation Grade B)**</mark>

Regarding **resection depth**, no high-level evidence is available to define an optimal plane. The project team recommends resection **down to the fascia**, provided the fascia itself is preserved.  

**(Recommendation Grade C)**

## <mark>Lichen Sclerosus</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Presentation</mark>
<mark>The most common symptom of lichen sclerosus is **pruritus**, which can range from mild to severe.</mark> The affected vulvar skin is fragile, and scratching often leads to painful erosions. <mark>By the time many women seek treatment, they already exhibit late-stage signs, including significant textural changes and scarring.</mark> Scarring may result in narrowing of the introitus, leading to dyspareunia or even intolerable pain during intercourse.

Lichen sclerosus typically begins with white **papules or plaques** that commonly appear first on the anterior vulva and periclitoral area. While these lesions may occasionally be smooth and waxy—especially on moist skin—the classic presentation features **hypopigmented, well-demarcated plaques** with a **cellophane paper-like texture**. The skin is generally thin and fragile, with frequent **erosions** and **purpura**. Some patients, particularly those with severe itching, develop **thickened, hyperkeratotic** skin.

### Chronic Changes
With long-standing disease, progressive **scarring** and **resorption** occur. Common findings include:
- Resorption of the **labia minora**
- Scarring and fusion of the **clitoral hood**, which may bury the clitoris
- Midline agglutination (as seen in late-stage disease)

### Extragenital Involvement
Extragenital lichen sclerosus affects a minority of patients and is most often found on the **upper trunk and arms**. These lesions typically occur on keratinized skin and are usually **asymptomatic**.

### Autoimmune Association
An association with circulating autoantibodies has been reported. However, the only autoimmune condition with sufficient evidence to warrant laboratory testing is **hypothyroidism**.

### <mark>Differential Diagnosis</mark>
Fully developed lichen sclerosus—with its characteristic **hypopigmentation**, **shiny or crinkled texture**, and **fragile skin**—is usually easily recognized. However, early or atypical cases may be subtle or mimic other dermatoses.

### <mark>Complications</mark>
- <mark>**Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the vulva** is a serious complication.</mark>
- <mark>Historically, 2% to 3% of untreated patients developed SCC, particularly those with chronic **hyperkeratosis** or **erosions**.</mark>
- <mark>With effective **topical glucocorticoid therapy**, the risk of malignancy is significantly reduced.</mark>

### Treatment
- **Midpotency topical glucocorticoids** may relieve symptoms but often fail to normalize skin texture or prevent scarring.
- **Ultrapotent glucocorticoids**, such as **clobetasol propionate ointment**, applied once or twice daily, typically alleviate symptoms within days.
- **Several months of treatment** (usually 3–5 months) are required for maximal clinical improvement.

### Maintenance and Monitoring
- Patients should be followed **monthly** during daily treatment to:
  - Monitor for **therapeutic response**
  - Watch for **steroid-induced side effects** (e.g., skin atrophy)
- Once improvement is achieved, the frequency of application should be gradually reduced to a **maintenance regimen**.
- <mark>**Long-term maintenance therapy** is typically necessary to prevent relapse.</mark>

# <mark>Comorbidities</mark>

In male patients, **lichen sclerosus (LS)** is associated with an increased body mass index and has been linked to **coronary artery disease**, **diabetes mellitus (DM)**, and **tobacco use**.

<mark>Diabetes mellitus and LS co-occur more frequently than expected by chance, leading some experts to recommend **screening for DM in patients with LS**.</mark>

Women with LS often report additional bladder, bowel, and pain-related conditions. In a cohort of 308 women with LS attending a vulval clinic, self-reported comorbidities included:
- **Overactive bladder** (15.3%)
- **Stress urinary incontinence** (27.9%)
- **Constipation** (32.5%)
- **Irritable bowel syndrome** (19.5%)
- **Thyroid dysfunction** (33.1%) — representing a 2- to 3-fold increased risk
- **Fibromyalgia** (9.1%)
- **Temporomandibular joint disorder** (13.0%)
- **Vulval pain** (83.1%)

A multicentre Italian study suggests that **metabolic factors**—including obesity, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and sedentary lifestyle—may contribute to the development of genital LS in genetically predisposed individuals, with a similar risk profile observed in both males and females.

Hu et al. compared women with vulval LS (n = 865) to those with other vulval conditions (n = 1118). **Increasing age**, **thyroid disease**, and **anorectal fissures** were significantly associated with vulval LS. The link between anorectal fissures and LS is likely a **sequela of the disease** rather than a true comorbidity.

<mark>An association between **genital melanoma** and LS has been reported in multiple case series, particularly in women.</mark> <mark>**Vulval melanoma** is rare, with an incidence of 0.10–0.13 per 100,000 individuals, typically affecting postmenopausal women.</mark> <mark>However, patients with LS appear to have an **increased risk** of developing vulval melanoma, including in rare cases among girls.</mark> <mark>Additionally, there is an elevated risk of **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)** in LS patients, which should be carefully monitored.</mark>

---

# EPIDEMIOLOGY

## Incidence/Prevalence

The exact prevalence of LS remains uncertain and is likely **underestimated**, partly due to underdiagnosis. It is a common condition seen in vulval and penile dermatology clinics. Alongside spongiotic dermatitis and other lichenoid interface dermatoses, LS accounts for the majority of foreskin specimens examined in pathology departments.

Estimated prevalence ranges from **0.1% in children** to **3% in women over 80 years**. Data from the Oxford clinic suggest an annual presentation rate of approximately **150–200 women per million population**. A recent study found that by age 80, **1.6% of women** will have developed LS. In males, the estimated incidence is **0.07%**, based on retrospective review of discharge records from a US Army Medical Center.

## Age at Onset

LS can develop at any age. The prevalence of **vulval LS increases with age**, with the highest frequency observed in **postmenopausal women**, although this may not be directly tied to menopausal status alone. Approximately **20% of affected women experience onset before menopause**.

A **second peak** in incidence is observed **before puberty**, with both peaks occurring during periods of **low oestrogen levels**. This has led to speculation that low oestrogen may play an aetiological role, possibly through modulation of immune responses—oestrogen tends to favor T-cell-mediated immunity over antibody-mediated responses. Alternatively, reduced lubrication during these periods may increase susceptibility to **mechanical trauma** (Koebner phenomenon).

Wallace described a **continuous rise in incidence from puberty to perimenopause**, peaking around menopause, followed by a decline. In men, incidence rises after puberty, possibly with a **prepubertal peak**, and decreases again after age 60. One study reported a near doubling of incidence in the third decade, which may reflect the military setting of the study, though a similar peak has also been observed in non-military populations.

## <mark>Late Lichen Sclerosus Findings and Management</mark>

<mark>The loss of labia minora and midline agglutination of the clitoral hood are commonly observed in advanced lichen sclerosus.</mark>

<mark>Topical therapy with ultrapotent glucocorticoids, such as **clobetasol propionate ointment** applied once or twice daily, typically alleviates symptoms within a few days.</mark> However, several months of continuous treatment are necessary for complete resolution of clinical findings.[24,25] Most patients require 3 to 5 months of daily application to achieve maximal improvement. <mark>Monthly follow-up during active treatment is recommended to monitor for both therapeutic response and potential steroid-induced side effects, allowing for timely tapering of application frequency.</mark>

As adjunctive therapy during the first one to two weeks, sedating doses of an **antihistamine** or a **tricyclic antidepressant** can help control pruritus and promote healing.

<mark>Lichen sclerosus is generally not cured by treatment, and long-term maintenance is often needed.</mark> <mark>One study reported an 84% recurrence rate after discontinuation of therapy.[26]</mark>

### <mark>Differential Diagnosis of Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus</mark>

#### <mark>Most Likely</mark>
- <mark>Lichen simplex chronicus</mark>  
- <mark>Lichen planus</mark>  
- <mark>Vitiligo</mark>

#### <mark>Consider</mark>
- <mark>Immunobullous disease</mark>  
- <mark>Contact dermatitis</mark>

#### <mark>Always Rule Out</mark>
- <mark>Squamous cell carcinoma</mark>

Despite the necessity for prolonged therapy, there is no established optimal maintenance regimen. Many patients maintain good control with thrice-weekly application of an ultrapotent topical glucocorticoid indefinitely.

<mark>No other treatment matches the rapid and significant efficacy of topical ultrapotent glucocorticoids.</mark> Alternative medical therapies have mostly been evaluated in open-label studies. **Tacrolimus**[27–29] and **pimecrolimus**[30–31] have shown effectiveness in some cases (see Chap. 235). Topical **testosterone**, **progesterone**, and **estrogen** have demonstrated minimal benefit—comparable to vehicle or lubricant alone[32–34]—and may even increase irritation.[35] **Topical tretinoin 0.025%** and **calcipotriol** may improve symptoms in certain patients, but their use is limited by potential irritation.[36,37] **Oral retinoids** have been beneficial in select cases.[38] Traditional Chinese medicine, including herbal remedies and acupuncture, has been widely reported in Chinese literature to improve symptoms.[39]

Surgical interventions such as **cryotherapy**, **vulvectomy**, **carbon dioxide laser vaporization**, **pulsed dye laser therapy**, and **photodynamic therapy** have been proposed for lichen sclerosus treatment.[40–44]

---

## Vulvar Fissures

Small linear fissures on the vulva are frequent causes of **itching**, **stinging**, and **dyspareunia**.[45] Clinically, they may appear as painful erythematous lines within skinfolds or as distinct linear erosions.

The most recognized type occurs at the **posterior fourchette**, where splitting during intercourse leads to sharp tearing pain followed by burning and stinging upon exposure to alkaline semen. Although healing is rapid, recurrence with coitus is common. The etiology remains unclear. The condition often arises suddenly after years of pain-free intercourse. Preventive measures include adequate lubrication and positioning the woman in the superior (on-top) position to reduce trauma. If conservative measures fail, **surgical excision (perineoplasty)** may be required—removing the vertical fissure and closing the defect with advancement of vaginal mucosa to cover the area.[46]

Recurrent fissuring within skinfolds, particularly in the **interlabial sulci**, is a common source of vulvar stinging and irritation. Women typically present with chronic discomfort exacerbated by friction or moisture.

## <mark>Non-autoimmune diseases</mark>

### <mark>Main differential diagnoses for DH: non-autoimmune diseases</mark>

Scabies  
Scabies may closely mimic the pruritic, vesicular, and papular lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), particularly in the early stages. <mark>The presence of burrows, preferential involvement of finger webs, wrists, elbows, and genitalia, and intense nocturnal itching are suggestive of scabies.</mark> A definitive diagnosis is achieved by identifying *Sarcoptes scabiei* mites, eggs, or fecal matter in skin scrapings examined under microscopy.

<mark>Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis</mark>  
<mark>These conditions can present with pruritic papules, vesicles, and erythematous plaques, resembling DH, especially when distributed on the elbows, knees, or buttocks.</mark> <mark>However, contact dermatitis typically correlates with exposure to specific allergens or irritants and lacks the symmetrical, chronic-relapsing pattern seen in DH.</mark> Patch testing can aid in identifying the responsible agent.

<mark>Atopic dermatitis</mark>  
<mark>Atopic dermatitis may present with pruritic, eczematous lesions that could be confused with the eczema-like variant of DH.</mark> <mark>However, atopic dermatitis usually affects flexural areas, has a personal or family history of atopy, and lacks the characteristic immunopathological findings of DH, such as granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae.</mark>

Arthropod bite reactions  
<mark>Reactions to insect bites can manifest as grouped or linearly arranged papules and vesicles (often referred to as "breakfast, lunch, and dinner" lesions), which may resemble the agminated vesicles of DH.</mark> A detailed history of outdoor exposure and the transient nature of bite reactions help differentiate them from the persistent, symmetrical lesions of DH.

<mark>Pityriasis lichenoides chronica</mark>  
This condition presents with recurrent crops of small, scaly, reddish-brown papules that may occasionally have a vesicular appearance. <mark>It typically affects the trunk and limbs and may be mistaken for the papulovesicular stage of DH.</mark> However, it lacks the intense pruritus and characteristic IgA deposition seen in DH.

<mark>Dyshidrotic eczema</mark>  
Also known as pompholyx, this condition is characterized by deep-seated vesicles on the palms, soles, and lateral aspects of the fingers—sites also commonly affected in DH. However, dyshidrotic eczema is not associated with gluten sensitivity and shows spongiosis and vesicle formation on histology without neutrophilic microabscesses or IgA deposits.

<mark>Drug eruptions</mark>  
Certain drug-induced eruptions (e.g., those caused by vancomycin, amphetamines, or anticonvulsants) can present with pruritic papulovesicular lesions resembling DH. A thorough medication history and resolution of lesions upon drug withdrawal support the diagnosis of a drug eruption. <mark>Additionally, these lack the specific immunopathological features of DH.</mark>
