# CHRONIC WOUNDS AND IMPAIRED HEALING

The previous discussion has focused on cutaneous wound repair following acute injury. <mark>However, the applicability of these processes is limited in the context of chronic wounds, such as those associated with diabetes, venous and arterial insufficiency, and conditions complicated by persistent inflammation or dysfunctional host responses.</mark> <mark>In chronic wounds, the linear, sequential progression through the phases of healing—hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling—is disrupted.</mark> <mark>There is no orderly transition between phases, and different areas of the same wound may be in different stages of repair simultaneously.</mark>

Acute wounds, such as surgical or traumatic injuries, follow a predictable healing timeline and typically resolve without complication. <mark>In contrast, chronic wounds are characterized by a failure to progress through the normal stages of healing, resulting in prolonged non-healing or impaired healing.</mark> Despite numerous observations and proposed hypotheses, studying the pathophysiology of chronic wounds remains challenging, primarily due to the lack of animal models that accurately replicate human impaired healing.

Some chronic wounds arise from a combination of ischemia, pressure, and infection. Diabetic foot ulcers exemplify this pathophysiologic triad. While the direct role of hyperglycemia in ulcer development remains debated, it is well established that hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function, increasing susceptibility to infection in diabetic patients. Additionally, "small vessel disease" in diabetes is now understood not as an obstructive process but as a functional microvascular abnormality. Revascularization of the diabetic foot is considered appropriate when large-vessel disease is present and distal perfusion is adequate.

<mark>Venous ulcers represent another example of impaired healing, independent of pressure or arterial insufficiency.</mark> <mark>The primary underlying defect is venous hypertension—defined as the failure of venous pressure in the lower extremities to decrease appropriately during muscle contraction and exercise.</mark> <mark>Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain how venous hypertension leads to ulceration or lipodermatosclerosis.</mark>

<mark>One hypothesis emphasizes the perivascular accumulation of fibrin due to impaired fibrinolysis, forming a "fibrin cuff" around dermal capillaries that may hinder nutrient and oxygen exchange.</mark> <mark>Another theory focuses on microvascular endothelial damage, leading to leakage of fibrinogen and other macromolecules into the dermis.</mark> <mark>This leakage may trap essential growth factors and signaling molecules, rendering them inaccessible for tissue repair or maintenance.</mark> <mark>Specifically, growth factors such as PDGF can be sequestered by leaked proteins like albumin, fibrinogen, and α₂-macroglobulin—a known scavenger of growth factors.</mark>

Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) play a crucial role in normal wound repair, particularly in keratinocyte migration and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. However, in chronic wounds, including venous ulcers, wound fluid contains elevated levels of MMPs. These excessive proteolytic enzymes degrade the ECM, as well as cytokines and growth factors, further impairing the healing process.

It is also important to recognize that the tissue surrounding chronic wounds is pathologically altered. These changes are driven by the underlying disease process or by the persistent failure to heal. A prominent clinical example is the fibrotic tissue surrounding venous ulcers, known as lipodermatosclerosis. Once established, lipodermatosclerosis creates a hostile environment for healing and serves as a common site for ulcer recurrence. Venous ulcers occurring within areas of lipodermatosclerosis are particularly difficult to treat and often require comprehensive management strategies targeting both the ulcer and the surrounding dysfunctional tissue.

# <mark>Pathophysiology of Chronic Venous Insufficiency and Venous Leg Ulcers</mark>

<mark>All structures of the venous system may contribute to chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) and consequently to the development of venous leg ulcers.</mark>

<mark>Varices initially develop due to alterations in the vein wall, leading to valvular incompetence in both the descending and ascending venous pathways.</mark>

While some studies report a higher prevalence of varicose veins in women, this may reflect selection bias, as women are more likely to seek medical evaluation for cosmetic concerns. Population-based studies generally show no significant sex difference in varicose veins. <mark>However, advanced chronic venous disease (CVD) affects both sexes equally and can progress to leg ulceration—the end stage of CVI.</mark> Venous leg ulceration has a lifetime prevalence of 1% and an active prevalence of 0.3% in the adult Western population, with increasing incidence with age. Ulceration in individuals under 60 is uncommon and often associated with severe deep venous insufficiency.

<mark>As CVI progresses, venous hypertension extends to the venules and capillaries.</mark> <mark>Elevated intracapillary pressure increases capillary filtration, resulting in fluid leakage and edema.</mark> Concurrently, high molecular weight proteins such as fibrin escape into the pericapillary space, forming visible "fibrin cuffs" around capillaries.

Initially, it was hypothesized that these fibrin cuffs impair oxygen diffusion, causing tissue anoxia and ulceration. However, this theory was challenged by findings of fibrin cuffs in other skin conditions without reduced transcutaneous oxygen tension. <mark>Alternative mechanisms include leukocyte trapping in capillaries and the release of free radicals, contributing to tissue damage.</mark>

<mark>The transmission of high venous pressure to the dermal microcirculation triggers a chronic inflammatory response.</mark> <mark>This involves cytokine and growth factor release, promoting leukocyte migration into the interstitium and perpetuating inflammation.</mark> <mark>This process underlies the dermal fibrosis and tissue remodeling characteristic of CVI.</mark>

Microscopic studies have also revealed capillary thrombosis in white atrophy and other cutaneous manifestations of CVI, suggesting microvascular occlusion as another potential contributor to ulcer formation. More recently, it has been proposed that fibrin cuffs may sequester growth factors rather than oxygen, thereby impairing wound healing by limiting growth factor availability at the ulcer site.

These interrelated mechanisms are integrated into the **Rotterdam model**, which summarizes the multifactorial pathogenesis of venous leg ulcers.

Some authors suggest that **biofilm formation** may also play a significant role in delaying healing in chronic venous ulcers.

## Risk Factors

**Obesity** is a recognized risk factor for venous leg ulcers. It can induce venous hypertension and subsequent ulceration even in the absence of valvular incompetence or venous obstruction. **Dependency**, due to immobility, impairs muscle pump function and leads to venous stasis and hypertension. In both scenarios, venous valves may remain structurally patent, emphasizing the need for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation.

Therefore, clinical examination should be supplemented with technical investigations, particularly **duplex ultrasound**, ideally performed by a physician in collaboration with a technician, to accurately assess venous function and guide management.

# Symptomatology

Venous leg ulcers may arise spontaneously or follow minor trauma. Patient symptoms can range from mild to severe. Contrary to traditional teaching, venous leg ulcers **can be painful**, particularly during the ulcerative phase of white atrophy or when complicated by infection.

## Tissue Alterations in Chronic Wounds

<mark>It should also be recognized that tissues around chronic wounds are not normal and are altered by the primary pathogenic mechanisms or by the inability to heal readily.</mark> <mark>Clinically, the best example of this is the intense fibrosis surrounding venous ulcers, termed **lipodermatosclerosis**.</mark> <mark>Once established, lipodermatosclerosis can lead to ulcer formation and becomes a site of frequent ulcer recurrence.</mark> <mark>Venous ulcers surrounded by lipodermatosclerosis are notably more difficult to heal.</mark>

This may be due to alterations in the cellular composition of non-healing wounds. Most evidence to date—largely because of the ease of culturing—focuses on wound fibroblasts. Ulcer fibroblasts are known to be **senescent** and unresponsive to certain cytokines and growth factors. For instance, venous ulcer fibroblasts show unresponsiveness to **TGF-β1** and **PDGF**. The impaired response to TGF-β1 is associated with decreased expression of type II TGF-β receptors, leading to reduced phosphorylation of key signaling proteins such as **Smad2**, **Smad3**, and **MAPK**.

Similarly, the synthetic activity of cells in diabetic ulcers may be dysregulated, resulting in chronic wounds being "stuck" in a particular phase of the repair process. Several of these cellular abnormalities have been closely linked to impaired healing capacity.

## Basic Standards of Care

### Arterial Ulcers
- **Vascular reconstruction** is essential for healing arterial ulcers. Without revascularization, interventions are temporary and often culminate in amputation, especially in inoperable patients.
- Necrotic, stable arterial ulcers with an overlying eschar should not be disturbed unless a vascular reconstructive plan is in place.

### Venous Ulcers
- <mark>**Leg elevation** and **compression therapy** are the cornerstones of treatment (see Chap. 175).</mark>
- **Contact dermatitis** is common in patients with venous disease; therefore, minimizing the use of topical agents is often necessary.
- **Pentoxifylline** has been evaluated in randomized trials for accelerating venous ulcer healing. Results are mixed, though higher doses (800 mg three times daily) may be more effective than the standard 400 mg three times daily. Its role as standard therapy remains uncertain.
- **Stanozolol**, an anabolic steroid, was effective in reducing induration in acute, painful lipodermatosclerosis when compression is intolerable, but it is no longer available.
- To prevent recurrence, **graduated elastic compression stockings** delivering ~40 mm Hg pressure at the ankle are currently the only proven medical intervention. These should be worn long-term to reduce ulcer recurrence and manage other manifestations of chronic venous disease.

### Diabetic Foot Ulcers
- The primary pathophysiological triad—**neuropathy, ischemia, and trauma**—drives the development and recurrence of foot ulcers in diabetes (see Chap. 152).
- **Glycemic control** and management of systemic complications (e.g., renal failure) are critical components of therapy.
- **Off-loading** is the cornerstone of local wound care for neuropathic ulcers.
- Patients with ulcers due to vascular insufficiency or mixed etiology (neuropathic and ischemic) require **prompt referral** for vascular assessment and surgical consultation.

In both cases, the venous valves can be patent. This is also one of the important reasons to combine the classical physical examination with technical investigations, especially duplex ultrasound techniques. The duplex examination is therefore best performed by the physician together with a technician.

## <mark>Symptomatology</mark>

<mark>The venous leg ulcer arises either 'spontaneously' or often after a minor trauma.</mark> <mark>The patient's complaints due to the ulcer may vary from mild to severe.</mark> <mark>Although many textbooks state otherwise, venous leg ulcers can indeed be painful.</mark> <mark>Pain is particularly prominent during the ulcerative phase of white atrophy or when additional factors such as infection are present.</mark>

<mark>Clinically, venous leg ulcer is part of chronic venous insufficiency (CVI).</mark> <mark>Patients with CVI develop various skin changes over time, including pigmentation, corona phlebectatica, white atrophy, and dermato- and liposclerosis.</mark> <mark>The exact percentage of patients who progress to symptomatic disease remains unknown, as this has never been adequately studied.</mark>

<mark>The venous ulcer is typically located on the medial side of the ankle, less commonly on the lateral side.</mark> <mark>A specific variant is ulceration in acroangiodermatitis of the forefoot, seen in patients with foot pump incompetence.</mark> <mark>If an ulcer is located elsewhere on the lower leg, non-venous causes should be strongly suspected.</mark>

<mark>The clinical features of CVI are well recognized.</mark> <mark>For completeness, they are listed here: varicosities, edema, corona phlebectatica, hyperpigmentation, dermato- and liposclerosis, white atrophy, secondary lymphedema, stasis dermatitis (more accurately termed eczema cruris in the context of CVI), and ulceration.</mark> <mark>Skin changes in venous insufficiency result from alterations in both macro- and microcirculation.</mark> <mark>It remains unclear why extensive dermato- and liposclerosis develop in some patients while others predominantly exhibit white atrophy.</mark> <mark>Local factors may contribute and require further investigation.</mark>

## Quality of Life

Venous ulcers significantly impact patients' lives and affect multiple domains of health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including bodily pain, health perception, mental health, social functioning, and vitality. Treatment and, in particular, healing of venous ulcers lead to marked improvements in these areas.

Although several disease-specific HRQOL instruments have been developed, studies have shown them to be suboptimal. Generic instruments such as the SF-36, SF-12, and EuroQoL-5D are currently recommended for assessing the impact on patients' lives. Today, healthcare systems increasingly require treatment evaluation that includes patient-reported outcomes.

## Chapter 2 – Diagnostics

### Introduction

The differential diagnosis of venous leg ulcer is broad. However, only a few conditions are commonly encountered. Establishing an accurate diagnosis promptly is essential, as different underlying causes require entirely different management strategies. Misdiagnosis can have serious consequences for the patient.

### Anamnesis

#### Scientific basis

A thorough anamnesis is indispensable. Many patients with leg ulcers have complex medical histories and comorbidities. However, high-quality studies evaluating the diagnostic value of specific anamnestic items are lacking.

#### Conclusion

| Level 4 | Good studies on the value of specific items for anamnesis are not available. |

# <mark>MALIGNANT FIBROUS DERMAL TUMORS</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>A group of uncommon and rare cutaneous tumors with varying degrees of malignant potential.</mark>  
Includes **dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans**, **atypical fibroxanthoma**, **malignant fibrous histiocytoma**, **fibrosarcoma**, and **epithelioid sarcoma**.  
<mark>Diagnosis is made by biopsy.</mark>  
- <mark>**Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP)** is a locally aggressive tumor with a high rate of local recurrence and rare metastases.</mark>  
- **Atypical fibroxanthoma** is an intermediate-grade neoplasm that usually arises on sun-damaged skin in the eighth decade.  
- **Malignant fibrous histiocytoma** represents a morphologic pattern shared by many poorly differentiated neoplasms.  
- **Epithelioid sarcoma** is a rare tumor that classically presents on the hands and fingers of young males and can mimic nonneoplastic inflammatory lesions.

---

## Etiology and Pathogenesis

The histogenesis of DFSP is uncertain: fibrohistiocytic, purely fibroblastic, and neural-related differentiation have all been hypothesized. <mark>A very sensitive, although non-specific, marker for DFSP is **CD34**.</mark> <mark>A distinctive cell population within normal nerves has been shown to express CD34, consistent with a possible neural-related histogenesis of DFSP.</mark> <mark>CD34 can help distinguish between DFSP and scar tissue in re-excision specimens.</mark>

<mark>At the molecular level, DFSP exhibits the reciprocal translocation **t(17;22)(q22;q13)**, producing a fusion of the *collagen type I α1* gene and the *platelet-derived growth factor B-chain* (*PDGFB*) gene.</mark> <mark>Current techniques permit sensitive and specific detection of these fusion transcripts in paraffin-embedded DFSP tumor specimens by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).</mark> <mark>Both fibrosarcomatous transformation of DFSP and some cases of superficial fibrosarcoma harbor these fusion transcripts, suggesting a close affinity between DFSP and fibrosarcoma.</mark>

---

## Clinical Findings

### History

<mark>DFSP is a slow-growing lesion that often presents on the trunk and proximal extremities.</mark> <mark>Due to its indolent onset, patients may present for evaluation when the tumor is several centimeters in size.</mark> The tumor is often misdiagnosed as a simple scar or cyst. It may grow to several centimeters in diameter and form large, infiltrative tumors. In a small subset of patients, there is a history of prior trauma at the site. DFSP has also been reported to arise in scars, including surgical, burn, and vaccination sites.

### Cutaneous Lesions

The clinical morphology of DFSP is variable. The most common presentation is a firm, indurated plaque, often skin-colored, with red-brown exophytic nodules (see Fig. 125-1A). It can also present as a nonprotuberant, atrophic, violaceous lesion resembling morphea, sclerosing basal cell carcinoma, anetoderma, or scar (see Fig. 125-2). Large nodular tumors may develop. The epidermis may be atrophic, and focal ulceration can occur. The most common site is the trunk, followed by the extremities. Approximately 15% of cases occur on the head and neck.

---

### Laboratory Tests

**Histopathology**: DFSP is diagnosed by skin biopsy.  
Microscopically, DFSP is characterized by fibroblastic spindle cells arranged in interlacing fascicles that intersect and bend at acute angles, producing a **storiform (starburst) pattern** (see Fig. 125-1B).

# <mark>Genetics: CDKN2A-CDK4-TP53 Pathway</mark>

<mark>Germline mutations in the chromosome 9p21 tumor suppressor gene, *CDKN2A* (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A), account for approximately 40% of hereditary melanoma cases (defined as ≥3 melanomas in one lineage) and confer a 76% lifetime risk of developing melanoma in the United States.</mark> <mark>This risk varies by geographic region, being higher in Australia and lower in Europe, consistent with ambient UV exposure levels.</mark> <mark>Individuals with germline *CDKN2A* mutations also have an increased risk of pancreatic cancer, with an estimated 15% lifetime risk.</mark>

<mark>Although bona fide deleterious point mutations in *CDKN2A* are relatively uncommon in primary melanoma tumors, somatic inactivation—particularly through homozygous deletions—may be underrecognized due to technical limitations in detection.</mark>

<mark>The *CDKN2A* gene encodes two distinct tumor suppressor proteins through alternative reading frames: **p16** (also known as **INK4a**) and **p14<sup>ARF</sup>**.</mark>

- <mark>**p16** functions as a cell cycle regulator by binding to and inhibiting cyclin-dependent kinases **CDK4** and **CDK6**. This inhibition prevents phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein, thereby blocking progression from G1 to S phase of the cell cycle.</mark>
- <mark>Loss or inactivation of p16 leads to unchecked CDK4/6 activity, resulting in Rb hyperphosphorylation, release of the E2F transcription factor, and uncontrolled entry into S phase—promoting cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis.</mark>

<mark>**CDK4** is the direct binding partner of p16.</mark> <mark>Hereditary mutations in *CDK4* are rare, with only a few families reported worldwide.</mark> <mark>However, somatic *CDK4* mutations have been identified in some melanoma cell lines.</mark> <mark>These mutations typically render CDK4 resistant to p16-mediated inhibition, producing a functional outcome equivalent to p16 loss.</mark>

<mark>The second protein product of *CDKN2A*, **p14<sup>ARF</sup>**, stabilizes the **p53** tumor suppressor by inhibiting **MDM2**, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes p53 degradation.</mark> <mark>Loss of p14<sup>ARF</sup> function leads to increased MDM2 activity, accelerated p53 degradation, and impaired DNA damage response.</mark>

<mark>Thus, inactivation of *CDKN2A* disrupts both the **Rb pathway** (via p16 loss) and the **p53 pathway** (via p14<sup>ARF</sup> loss), effectively deregulating two major tumor suppressor networks.</mark> <mark>This dual impact likely explains the relatively low frequency of direct *TP53* mutations in melanoma, as p53 function is already compromised through upstream mechanisms.</mark>

---

# RAS Signaling Pathway

In 2002, Davies et al. reported somatic mutations in the *BRAF* gene in 66% of melanomas. *BRAF* encodes **B-raf**, a serine/threonine kinase that plays a central role in the **Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK** (MAPK) signaling pathway, which regulates cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation in response to extracellular signals such as growth factors, cytokines, and hormones.

Activation of this pathway proceeds as follows:
1. Extracellular ligands activate receptor tyrosine kinases.
2. This triggers **Ras** (a G-protein) to exchange GDP for GTP, activating it.
3. Active Ras recruits and activates **Raf** (including B-raf).
4. Raf phosphorylates and activates **MEK**, which then phosphorylates **ERK** (extracellular signal-regulated kinase).
5. Activated ERK translocates to the nucleus and regulates transcription factors involved in cell cycle progression.

Humans express three Raf isoforms: **A-raf**, **B-raf**, and **C-raf**. Among these, **B-raf** has the highest basal kinase activity. Activating somatic mutations in *BRAF* are common in melanoma, as well as in colorectal, ovarian, and papillary thyroid carcinomas, underscoring its role as a key oncogenic driver.

The most prevalent *BRAF* mutation in melanoma is **V600E**, which results in constitutive kinase activity and persistent MAPK pathway signaling, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation.

*BRAF* mutations are significantly more frequent in melanomas arising on skin with **intermittent sun exposure**. Notably, **81% of melanomas on skin without chronic sun damage** harbor either *BRAF* or *NRAS* mutations, highlighting the importance of MAPK pathway activation in this molecular subtype.

# Medical treatments

Regular reviews play a crucial role in enhancing patient compliance with treatment, which is a key factor in the success of androgenetic alopecia (AGA) management. Since visible results may take several months, maintaining adherence to therapy is essential.

Generally, with medical treatment, a reduction in hair loss becomes noticeable after 3–6 months, and visible hair regrowth typically appears after 6–12 months. Continuous, long-term treatment is required to sustain benefits. It is important to note that current medical treatments are not curative. Patients should be clearly informed about the limitations of therapy: AGA treatment cannot restore hair to prepubertal density, and the primary goal is to halt or slow further hair loss.

## Males

<mark>Two agents are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of AGA in men: **topical minoxidil** and **oral finasteride**.</mark>

### (1) Topical minoxidil solution

Topical minoxidil is applied as 1 mL of solution twice daily. Its exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is believed to prolong the anagen (growth) phase and increase hair shaft diameter, regardless of the underlying cause of hair loss.

The efficacy of minoxidil varies across studies. It is well established that the **5% formulation** is more effective than 2% or 3% solutions. In a study of men aged 18–49 years, those using 5% minoxidil had **45% higher hair counts** compared to those using the 2% solution. A Japanese study also demonstrated the superiority of 5% over 1% minoxidil in Japanese men, and a phase 4, open-label, multicenter trial confirmed the safety and efficacy of 5% minoxidil in Korean men with AGA.

Patients should be advised that during the first 2–8 weeks of treatment, a temporary increase in hair shedding may occur due to telogen effluvium. This is self-limiting and resolves as new anagen hairs begin to grow. It should not prompt discontinuation of treatment.

An advancement in minoxidil delivery is the **5% topical foam**, which has been shown in placebo-controlled, double-blind trials to be effective, safe, and cosmetically acceptable. The hydroalcoholic foam formulation offers convenience and improved tolerability for some patients.

### <mark>(2) Oral finasteride</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is a selective inhibitor of type II 5α-reductase, administered at a dose of **1 mg daily**.</mark> <mark>Clinical trials in men aged 18–41 years over a 2-year period reported the following outcomes:</mark>

- <mark>At **1 year**:</mark>  
  <mark>- 48% experienced hair regrowth (slight: 30%, moderate: 16%, great: 2%)</mark>  
  <mark>- 51% had stabilized hair loss</mark>  
  <mark>- 1% showed progressive hair loss</mark>  

- <mark>At **2 years**:</mark>  
  <mark>- 66% had regrowth</mark>  
  <mark>- 33% had stabilized hair loss</mark>  
  <mark>- 1% continued to lose hair</mark>  

<mark>The number of responsive hairs typically stabilizes after 1 year, but continued treatment improves hair length, thickness, and pigmentation, leading to better scalp coverage over time.</mark> <mark>Upon discontinuation, regrown hair is gradually lost, and the balding process resumes.</mark>

An extension of this study to 5 years confirmed that finasteride 1 mg/day is well tolerated and provides durable improvements in hair growth.

Finasteride is generally safe, with most side effects being mild and not requiring treatment cessation. Rare adverse effects include decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.

Currently, there is **no proven benefit** of finasteride in women with AGA. A placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal Western women using 1 mg/day for 1 year showed no significant improvement. However, a study using **5 mg/day** in Asian women suggested potential benefit for normoandrogenic women with female pattern hair loss (FPHL). Further research is needed to define the role of finasteride in female patients.

## <mark>Treatment of Pattern Hair Loss</mark>

The latter group is important to identify, as these patients are unlikely to be satisfied with treatments aimed at restoring hair growth, and involvement of other healthcare professionals—such as a clinical psychologist—may be necessary. <mark>Treatments for pattern hair loss are available, but patients should be counseled that none will restore hair growth to its prepubertal density.</mark> <mark>While some recovery of hair growth is possible, the primary goal of medical treatments is to prevent further progression (see Box 86-2).</mark>

---

### Men

<mark>Two medical treatments—**topical minoxidil solution (TMS)** and **oral finasteride**—are licensed for the treatment of male pattern hair loss and can be used in combination.</mark> <mark>A trial of at least 6 months is required to assess efficacy, and treatment must be continued indefinitely to maintain results.</mark>

#### Box 86-2: Treatment of Androgenetic Alopecia

<mark>**General Principle:**</mark>  
<mark>Caution against unrealistic expectations; the primary goal is to halt disease progression.</mark>

<mark>**Male Pattern Hair Loss:**</mark>
- <mark>**5% topical minoxidil solution or foam**, applied twice daily</mark>  
- <mark>**Oral finasteride**, 1 mg daily</mark>  
- <mark>**Combination therapy**: Use for at least 6 months to assess response; continue treatment to maintain benefits</mark>  
- **Surgery (e.g., hair transplantation)**: Most effective for restoring frontal hair loss

**Female Pattern Hair Loss:**
- <mark>**2%–5% topical minoxidil solution**, applied twice daily</mark>  
- **Topical 17β-estradiol** (e.g., estradiol benzoate, 20–25 mg/mL in isopropanol)  
- **Oral anti-androgens** (e.g., spironolactone, cyproterone acetate)  
- **Combination therapy**: Use for at least 6 months to assess response; continue treatment to maintain benefits  
- Maintain **serum ferritin >40 μg/L**  
- <mark>**Hair transplantation** in selected cases</mark>

---

### MINOXIDIL

<mark>Clinical trials using various endpoints—including hair counts, hair weight, and global photography—have shown that up to 60% of men experience improvement in vertex balding with 5% topical minoxidil, with a mean increase in hair density of 10% to 12%.</mark> <mark>Response rates with 2% minoxidil are lower.</mark> <mark>Treatment must be continued to sustain results; any gains are typically lost within 4 to 6 months after discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>Minoxidil is not effective for frontotemporal recession.</mark> <mark>Scalp irritation may occur, most commonly due to propylene glycol in the formulation.</mark>

---

### <mark>FINASTERIDE</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is a type 2 5α-reductase inhibitor.</mark> <mark>At a dose of 1 mg daily, it prevents progression of hair loss in most men.</mark> <mark>After 2 years of treatment, approximately two-thirds show some improvement in hair growth.</mark> <mark>In long-term studies, a slight decline in hair count was observed after 5 years, but hair loss progressed more rapidly in untreated individuals.</mark>

<mark>A small but statistically significant increase in sexually related adverse effects—such as impotence—has been reported; however, finasteride is otherwise well-tolerated.</mark> <mark>Any benefit is lost within 12 months of stopping treatment.</mark>

<mark>The exact mechanism of action in responders remains unclear.</mark> <mark>Recent evidence suggests that finasteride may reactivate "hypotrophic" terminal hair follicles by promoting faster entry into and prolonging the anagen phase, rather than inducing true vellus-to-terminal hair conversion.</mark>

<mark>Despite a lack of formal clinical trials, **combination therapy with topical minoxidil and oral finasteride** is commonly used in practice.</mark> <mark>Dual inhibition of both type 1 and type 2 5α-reductase may offer additional benefit in treating male pattern hair loss.</mark>

---

### SURGERY

Various surgical techniques exist for male pattern hair loss, with **hair transplantation** being the most widely used. These procedures redistribute existing terminal hairs to balding areas, without increasing the total number of terminal hairs. When performed by experienced surgeons and with appropriate patient selection, excellent cosmetic outcomes can be achieved.

Surgery is the only treatment capable of improving hair coverage on completely bald scalp and can rapidly restore hair. It is particularly effective for frontal hair loss (see Chap. 250).

---

### Women

(Continued section—content likely follows on female pattern hair loss, including specific considerations for diagnosis, treatment response, and management strategies.)

# Overview of common therapeutic options

<mark>Table 4 provides a summary of evidence level, efficacy in preventing progression and/or improving androgenetic alopecia (AGA), safety, and practicability for the most commonly used therapeutic interventions.</mark> The table is intended to offer a preliminary orientation. <mark>However, an individualized treatment approach is essential, taking into account each patient’s clinical condition, expectations, needs, and concerns.</mark> The optimal therapy should be decided jointly by the physician and patient, considering the best available evidence, expected outcomes, ease of use, and likelihood of adherence.

# Minoxidil

## <mark>Efficacy – males</mark>

<mark>Forty-eight studies evaluating minoxidil’s efficacy in men with AGA met the inclusion criteria.</mark> <mark>The majority of these studies provided grade A2 (n = 22) or grade B (n = 18) evidence, with eight rated as grade C, resulting in an overall **evidence level 1**.</mark>

- <mark>Minoxidil 2% solution applied twice daily is effective in preventing progression and improving AGA in the frontotemporal and vertex regions (evidence level 1).</mark>
- <mark>Minoxidil 5% solution or foam applied twice daily is more effective than the 2% formulation (evidence level 2).</mark>

<mark>One study using oral minoxidil at 5 mg/day in men showed increased hair count, though the improvement was only marginally greater than that seen with topical minoxidil.</mark> <mark>However, oral administration was associated with notable side effects, including hypertrichosis (93%), pedal edema (10%), and ECG changes (10%).</mark>

## <mark>Efficacy – females</mark>

<mark>Nineteen studies on topical minoxidil in women with AGA were included.</mark> <mark>Seven provided grade A2 evidence, nine grade B, and three grade C, leading to an overall **evidence level 1**.</mark>

- <mark>Minoxidil 2% solution applied twice daily is effective in preventing progression and improving AGA in women (evidence level 1).</mark>
- <mark>Minoxidil 5% solution or foam applied once daily shows comparable efficacy to the 2% solution applied twice daily (evidence level 2).</mark>

## <mark>Instructions for use, practicability, and side effects</mark>

- <mark>Apply 1 mL of solution (using a pipette) or half a cap of foam to dry hair and scalp, twice daily in men and once daily in women.</mark>
- <mark>When using a spray, ensure even distribution over affected areas.</mark>
- <mark>Treatment response should be evaluated after 6 months. If effective, ongoing use is required to maintain benefits.</mark>

<mark>Patients should be informed about transient increased telogen shedding during the first few months of treatment.</mark> <mark>Discontinuation of minoxidil typically leads to resumption of hair loss.</mark>

<mark>Common side effects:</mark>
- <mark>**Hypertrichosis**, likely due to local spread, excessive application, or individual sensitivity.</mark>
- <mark>**Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis**, more frequently associated with the 5% solution due to its propylene glycol content. Allergic reactions to propylene glycol or minoxidil can be confirmed via patch testing.</mark>

<mark>Due to insufficient safety data, topical minoxidil should be discontinued during pregnancy and lactation.</mark>

## Combination therapies – males and females

Nine studies in men and six in women compared topical minoxidil monotherapy with combination treatments.

- In men: Three studies provided grade A2 evidence and six grade B. However, due to limited data per specific combination (only one or two studies each), the overall evidence level is **3**.
- In women: Three studies provided grade B evidence and three grade C, also resulting in **evidence level 3**.

For detailed results on specific combinations, refer to the full guideline document.

## Hair Transplantation

<mark>The success of hair transplantation depends on the availability of sufficient permanent donor hair and the absence of overlying diffuse telogen effluvium (Table 8).</mark>

Final results can be assessed at 9–12 months post-procedure. In many cases, multiple surgical sessions are necessary to achieve optimal outcomes.

The best long-term results are observed in patients with medically controlled or spontaneously stabilized androgenetic alopecia (AGA). <mark>In men, combining **finasteride 1 mg** and/or **topical minoxidil** with **follicular unit transplantation** may help reduce postoperative progression of AGA.</mark>

**Body dysmorphic disorder** or **unrealistic patient expectations** are contraindications for this aesthetic procedure.

---

## Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP)

### Efficacy – Males

Two studies evaluating PRP efficacy in male and female patients with AGA met the inclusion criteria for the guideline, both providing grade C evidence, resulting in a level of evidence 3.¹⁰⁵,¹⁰⁶

### Efficacy – Females

Three studies assessing PRP in female patients were included in the evidence-based evaluation.¹⁰⁵–¹⁰⁷ Two of these studies included both male and female participants, with one study enrolling only two women.¹⁰⁵,¹⁰⁶ The levels of evidence were graded as B, C, and C, leading to an overall level of evidence 3.

Increases in hair density were reported across the studies. However, limitations include small sample sizes, heterogeneous PRP protocols, lack of control groups, and pooled reporting of results for men and women in two of the three studies. Except for one study, long-term follow-up data are lacking.

Based on current evidence, there is **limited support** for the use of PRP in treating AGA in both men and women (Table 9).

### Instructions for Use / Practicability / Side Effects

There is **no standardized protocol** for PRP treatment in AGA. Techniques for platelet isolation and activation, as well as dosage, injection frequency, and treatment intervals, vary significantly across studies and clinical practices. This lack of standardization limits comparability and reproducibility.

# The Battered Child

<mark>Bruising is the result of blunt trauma, delivered either accidentally or intentionally.</mark> Active children, particularly toddlers, are prone to multiple bruises, and the identification of abusive injury is fraught with difficulty. <mark>The size, shape, color, and feel of a bruise varies based on anatomic site, the degree of force used, the firmness of the object delivering the force, and the underlying health of the injured individual.</mark> Great care and attention to detail must be exercised when evaluating these children, who are often brought to the office for an unrelated complaint. The history should include as much detail as possible regarding the onset, mechanism, and progression of injuries.

## Conditions Mistaken for Abusive Bruising

- <mark>True petechiae and purpura</mark>  
- <mark>Disorders of coagulation</mark>  
- <mark>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</mark>  
- Infections  
  - Rocky Mountain spotted fever  
  - Meningococcal infections  
  - Group A streptococcal infections  
- Palpable purpura of vasculitis  
- Valsalva petechiae  
- Lichen sclerosus  
- Folk remedies  
  - Cao gio: vigorous rubbing with a hard object such as a coin  
  - Cupping: suction mark left by the cooling of a warm metal cup  
- Nodular lesions mimicking deep bruises  
  - Neuroblastoma  
  - Vascular malformations  
  - Dermatomyositis-associated nodules  
- Discolorations that look like bruises  
  - Phytophotodermatitis  
  - Maculae caeruleae from lice infestation  
  - Mongolian spots  
  - Dye from blue jeans  
- Inflammatory conditions that mimic bruising  
  - Urticaria, angioedema, urticarial vasculitis  
  - Pernio  
- Conditions that mimic whip marks  
  - Incontinentia pigmenti  
  - Striae  
  - Phytophotodermatitis  

## Conditions Mistaken for Nonaccidental Burns

- Phytophotodermatitis  
- Folk remedies (Maquas, or moxibustion): burns delivered near diseased organs or therapeutic sites as in acupuncture  
- Impetigo  
- Epidermolysis bullosa  
- Immunobullous diseases  
- Sunburn, xeroderma pigmentosum  
- Burns from objects heated by the sun  
- Electric burn from an enuresis blanket  
- Chemical burns from:  
  - Undiluted acetic acid  
  - Icy Hot balm  
  - Calcium chloride  
- Diaper dermatitis  
- Pernio  
- Fixed drug eruption  

Ideally, there should be an abuse team consisting of a dermatologist, pediatrician, social worker, medical photographer, and, when needed, pediatric subspecialists such as orthopedists, hematologists, psychologists, and gynecologists. It is most helpful if a relationship is established with the abuse team before an abuse incident occurs, and a clear protocol for managing suspected or alleged abuse is in place within the practitioner’s office. Local emergency numbers for reporting child abuse can be obtained from the Child Welfare Information Gateway or Childhelp National Headquarters.

Child abuse affects children across all ages, races, and socioeconomic classes. However, children who are more vulnerable to abuse are typically between 5 and 15 years of age and may have emotional or behavioral problems, special medical needs, multiple siblings, live in single-parent households, or reside at or below the poverty level. Abuse is approximately twice as common among Pacific Islander, American Indian, Native Alaskan, and African American children compared to the general U.S. population. Perpetrators often have emotional or psychological difficulties, a history of being abused themselves, substance use disorders, a history of domestic violence or marital conflict, poor parenting skills, and low self-esteem. While these risk factors are informative, it is critical to remember that any child may be a victim of abuse, regardless of background or circumstance.
